Even a villain, his body weary from subjection to self-interest,
is compassionate toward those who have previously done him a favor.
A good person, even when provoked by a slanderer, does not think inwardly
of any evil or hostile thing.
Even the rays of the moon, though their leading portions fall upon the enemy of the sun (<s>Rāhu</s>),
scatter only nectar.
A person of good family, even when angered, does not utter what should not be spoken;
sugarcane, even when pressed, yields only sweetness.
A base person, even when served with a hundred virtues,
says in jest what should be said only in quarrel.
Let the skilled in statecraft censure or praise;
let <s>Lakṣmī</s> (fortune) come or go as she pleases;
let death come today or at the end of an age —
the resolute do not move a step from the righteous path.
Without any motive and far beyond what is fitting, the great-souled, inherently noble,
clearly undertake the weightiest of tasks.
Rising up, did not the glorious <s>Agastya</s> drink the lord of rivers
with his garlands of waves, though it was more than a hundred pots' worth?
'A righteous and just conduct — hard to maintain even when life is at stake,
the wicked are not to be petitioned, even a friend of meager wealth is not to be importuned,
in misfortune one must stand tall, and the footsteps of the great are to be followed' —
by whom was this razor's-edge vow of the good prescribed?
Giving in secret, bustling hospitality when a guest arrives at the home,
no arrogance in prosperity, not belittling the stories of others,

children.text: priyaṃ kṛtvā maunaṃ sadasi kathanaṃ cāpyupakṛteḥ
children.translated_text: silence after doing a kindness, and in assembly speaking only of the favors [of others],
and extreme attachment to learning — these declare a person to be of noble birth.
At whose command does the seven-horsed sun dispel the darkness of the people?
For the sake of shade, by whom were the trees on the road made to fold their hands?
By whom are the clouds, shedding drops of water, implored for rain?
By their very nature, the good are girded for the service of others.
Its own abundance of fruit causes the tree's branches to break;
even the tail-feathers of a peacock make its movement sluggish;

children.text: caturagamano yo jātyāśvaḥ sa gauriva vāhyate
children.translated_text: a horse of four gaits, by its very nature, is yoked like an ox —

children.text: guṇavati jane prāyeṇaite guṇāḥ khalu vairiṇaḥ //
children.translated_text: among virtuous people, their very virtues are mostly their enemies.

children.text: khyātiṃ yatra guṇā na yānti guṇinastatrādaraḥ syātkutaḥ
children.translated_text: Where virtues achieve no fame, how can the virtuous win regard there?
What can even a well-learned man do among people turned to stone?
Even the charming sigh of a passionate woman, her voice turned away in intoxication,

children.text: sītkāro hi manoharopi badhire kiṃ nāma kuryādguṇam //
children.translated_text: beautiful though it be — what virtue can it achieve in the deaf?
The petty are in their thousands, occupied solely with the business of feeding themselves;

children.text: svārtho yasya parārtha eva sa pumānekaḥ satāmagraṇīḥ /
children.translated_text: he whose self-interest is itself the interest of others — that man alone is the leader of the good.
The submarine fire drinks the ocean to fill its insatiable belly,
but the rain-cloud acts to relieve the suffering of the world scorched by summer's heat.
Rising by their humility, proclaiming their own virtues through praise of others' merits,
nourishing their own interests while constantly engaged in great endeavors for others' sake,
tormenting the hostile-faced ones who shower harsh and abusive words upon them — merely by their patience —

children.text: santaḥ sāścaryacaryā jagati bahumatāḥ kasya nābhyarthanīyāḥ //
children.translated_text: the good, whose conduct is wondrous, honored in the world — who would not seek them?
The good alone spread abroad the excellence of the virtuous;
it is the winds that carry the fragrance of flowers to all directions.
Only the good person is skilled in savoring the nectar of virtue;
the cuckoo alone is skilled in relishing the fresh mango shoots.
Generally, the wise are worthy of instruction, not those of dull minds;
sesame seeds absorb the fragrance of flowers, but barley never does.
The heart of the spirited person achieves serenity through austerity itself;
a mirror, by rubbing with ash, mostly gains greater clarity.
The noble can endure the agitation of hardship, not the other;
it is the jewel that can withstand the grinding of the great whetstone, not a clod of earth.

children.text: jaḍe prabhavati prāyo duḥkhaṃ bibhrati sādhavaḥ /
children.translated_text: In the dull, suffering mostly prevails; the good bear [others' suffering];
when the white-rayed moon rises, the lotuses bear the anxiety of closing.
The difference between virtues is discerned mostly by the connoisseur, not by others;
the nose knows the scent of jasmine and <s>mallikā</s>, not the eye.
The good do not abandon their nature even through association with the wicked;

children.text: na tyajanti rutaṃ mañju kākasaṃparkataḥ pikāḥ //
children.translated_text: cuckoos do not give up their sweet song because of association with crows.
In prosperity, the heart of the good is tender; in adversity, it is hard;

children.text: sukumāraṃ madhau pattraṃ taroḥ syātkaṭhinaṃ śucau //
children.translated_text: the leaf of a tree is soft in spring and tough in summer.
The virtuous person does not inwardly abandon his nature even when fallen upon calamity;
camphor, even when consumed by fire, assumes its fragrance all the more.
Even the time of calamity for the good attains to what is praiseworthy;
even the time of <s>Rāhu</s>'s assault — the calamity of the moon — is beautiful.
Having seen the villainy of the wicked, one takes delight in the company of the good;
having climbed a mountain, the traveler finds ample satisfaction upon reaching the plain.
The noble are not attached to enjoyments that perish in a moment and lead to ruin;
swans, forsaking the filaments of the lotus, do not eat moss.

children.text: adhamaṃ bādhate bhūyo duḥkhāvego na tūttamam /
children.translated_text: The force of suffering afflicts the base greatly, but not the noble.
The touch of cold quickly pains the hands and feet, but not the eyes.
One who is virtuous and long-enduring is not tolerated even by fate;
the moon, glorious and full-orbed, remains so for but a single night.
A man of virtue shines everywhere; in any place he is foremost;
a gem adorns the head, the throat, the arm, and even the footstool.
Calamities do not long overwhelm the excellent;
the shadow cast by <s>Rāhu</s>'s eclipse upon the moon lasts but a moment.
The noble is satisfied by praise, the base by great wealth;
the gods are pleased by <s>japa</s> (prayers), and the spirits by offerings.
The minds of the virtuous never incline toward sinful deeds;
even when quickly [poured] into water, ghee would return to its solidified state.
Only certain fortunate persons in this world are worthy of refinement;
even when born of the same species, at the same age, and possessing the same intellect —
here is the clear proof: through familiarity and practice,

children.text: śukaḥ ślokānvaktuṃ prabhavati na kākaḥ kvacidapi //
children.translated_text: the parrot can recite verses, but a crow — never.
Even wealth given by others causes pain to those possessing propriety,
while the very same thing produces joy in the hearts of others;
a drop of sandalwood paste irritates the eye,
yet that same drop produces delight elsewhere on the body.
Of one born in a noble lineage, who alleviates sorrow, well-rounded,
pure of soul, an ornament of the entire world —
even a flaw born by chance in a virtuous person
necessarily becomes a virtue, like the hole in a pearl.
The home is crowded with destitute relatives; the teacher's house with arrogant students;
the market with city-swindlers; the hermitages with curse-ready ascetics;
the forest with lions and the like; the king's court with rogues; the horizons with thieves —
seeing everything thus crowded, where shall the honest, straightforward virtuous man find rest?
The exalted in virtue do not speak words that are proud, improbable,
improper, unpleasant, or pained by humiliation and suffering.
The good fortune of a virtuous person who extols the merits of others increases greatly;
the splendor of the moon shines with doubled beauty when the water-lilies bloom.
Even for the virtuous, the recognition of their own nature comes only from others;
for the reflection of one's own glory comes to the eyes only upon the surface of a mirror.
What is a burden of ten million to the capable? What is distance to the resolute?

children.text: ko videśaḥ savidyānāṃ kaḥ paraḥ priyavādinām //
children.translated_text: What is a foreign land to the learned? Who is a stranger to the sweet-spoken?

children.text: aśvaḥ śastraṃ śāstraṃ vīṇā vāṇī naraśca nārī ca /
children.translated_text: A horse, a weapon, a scripture, a lute, speech, a man, and a woman —
depending on the particular person they serve, they become either worthy or unworthy.
Endowed with enthusiasm, not given to procrastination,
skilled in the proper method of action, unattached to vices,
brave, grateful, and of firm friendship —
<s>Lakṣmī</s> (Fortune) herself wishes to dwell with such a one.
Even when ill-treated, the nature-born virtue of the magnanimous
cannot be wiped away;
even when a fire is held face-down,
its flames never go downward.
Justice is abandoned by the wicked, <s>dharma</s> has wavered,

children.text: kālaḥ kaliḥ kaluṣa eva paraṃ pravṛttaḥ /
children.translated_text: the age is <s>Kali</s>, nothing but corruption has advanced;
generally the wicked are ascendant,
and the virtuous, helpless, are merely objects of contempt.
In observance, no quarreling; in discrimination, no confusion;
in truth, no suspicion; in discipline, no deviation;
in virtue, no disrespect; in skill, no obstruction;
in <s>dharma</s>, no opposition — thus does the virtuous person act.
He is to be honored among men, to be celebrated by the gods,
through deeds of compassion, merit, and service;
he whose body is adorned with the ornament of benefiting others
attains the essential purpose of worldly existence.
Whether he serves the water-lily without discrimination, or whether the bee
comes from the hostile lotus — either way,
the ceaseless sequence of serving others and one's own, of the virtuous,
is sweet without [calculated] intention.
Those [qualities] which, when proclaimed before people, make one seem boastful,
and which, even when not proclaimed, cause some inner pain —
which, when throbbing in the heart and clinging to the throat, are somehow to be told —
only the blessed find a true friend for that purpose.

children.text: udanvacchinnā bhūḥ sa ca nidhirapāṃ yojanaśataṃ
children.translated_text: The earth is bounded by the ocean; that reservoir of waters [stretches] a hundred <s>yojanas</s>;
the sun, always a traveler, proclaims the measure of the sky;
thus, most entities display clearly defined boundaries;
but the awakening of the wisdom of the virtuous — that is boundless and triumphs!
They do not become angry even with those who have offended; they help even [them] with compassion;
they do not seek awareness even of their own [goodness] — such are those capable of uplifting the world.
It purifies the vessel, does not diminish virtues,

children.text: snehaṃ na saṃharati nāpi malaṃ prasūte /
children.translated_text: does not withdraw affection, nor does it produce impurity;
beautiful at the end of faults, it does not partake of unsteadiness —
the company of the virtuous is a certain lamp in the abode of good fortune.
Even a tiny gem can save the life of one who has swallowed poison;
even the cub of a lioness, in fury, challenges elephants;
even a small fire, arising from a tree-trunk, burns the forest —
the innate splendor of the naturally great does not depend on bodily form.

children.text: namaḥ khalebhyaḥ ka ivāthavā na tā-
children.translated_text: Obeisance to the wicked! For who that wishes to live
would not sufficiently salute them here?
They who, without any fault [on the victim's part], like great sages,
can hurl people to the netherworld with a curse!

children.text: viṣadharatopyativiṣamaḥ khala iti na mṛṣā vadanti vidvāṃsaḥ /
children.translated_text: The learned do not speak falsely when they say the wicked one is worse than a venomous serpent;
for he is the enemy of the mongoose (protector), always the enemy of families, and ever a slanderer.

children.text: atimaline kartavye bhavati khalānāmatīva nipuṇā dhīḥ /
children.translated_text: In executing extremely vile deeds, the intellect of the wicked is exceedingly sharp;

children.text: timire hi kauśikānāṃ rūpaṃ pratipadyate dṛṣṭiḥ //
children.translated_text: for in darkness, the sight of owls attains [its full] keenness.
When the virtues of others are destroyed, the impurity of the wicked becomes extreme;
even when the moon's light is obscured, the darkness of rain-clouds increases further.

children.text: hasta iva bhūtimalino laṅghayati yathā yathā khalaḥ sūjanam /
children.translated_text: The more the wicked one transgresses against the virtuous — like a soiled hand —

children.text: darpaṇamiva taṃ kurute tathā tathā nirmalacchāyam //
children.translated_text: the more he makes [the virtuous one] shine clearly, as [a soiled hand makes] a mirror [shine when wiped].
Bowing down when seizing a livelihood, rising up again after obtaining it —

children.text: kiṃ kaniṣṭhā uta jyeṣṭhā ghaṭīyantrasya durjanāḥ //
children.translated_text: are they the younger or the elder buckets of the waterwheel? [No,] they are the wicked!
To one always worthy of being broken, filled with chaff inside —
homage to the wicked one — and to the mortar — both possessed of many seeds!
His tongue defiles worthy recipients; he seeks morsels; he is fierce in quarrels;
always impure, the slanderer truly resembles a dog.
Alas! The wicked, though unlearned, is a scholar by merit of [others'] merit;
in proclaiming his own virtues, he is a <s>Śeṣa</s> (the Remainder); in slandering others, a lord of speech!
In slandering the virtuous, the wicked one — everywhere eyes, head, and mouth —
everywhere ears, in the world, stands pervading everything.
When virtuous deeds are spoken of, the tongue of the fool, afflicted with the disease of envy in the throat,
does not move even when pulled by a crane's beak.
Made of <s>māyā</s> (illusion) by nature, agitated by passion, hatred, and pride,
the wicked one is like <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) itself — delusive even to the great.
Even a variegated picture the deceiver produces effortlessly;

children.text: laghuśca mahatāṃ madhye tasmātkhala iti smṛtaḥ //
children.translated_text: he is light amidst the great — therefore he is called <s>khala</s> (wicked).
With the wicked, drunk with wealth, the base in power,

children.text: piśunena padasthena hā praje kva gamiṣyasi //
children.translated_text: the slanderer in office — alas, O people, where will you go?
A hundred deeds done for the undeserving are lost; a hundred fine sayings are lost on the foolish;
a hundred words are lost on the unresponsive; a hundred insights are lost on the insensible.
A gift to an unworthy recipient is lost; good counsel given without appreciation is lost;
virtue is lost on one who does not know virtue; courtesy is lost on the ungrateful.
From afar, hand raised; eyes moist; half-rising from his seat;
eager for a tight embrace; prompt in response to questions about dear topics —
poison hidden within, honey without, and exceedingly full of deceit —
what is this unprecedented theatrical performance taught by the wicked?
Those who strive to destroy the hard-won [achievements] of the great —
those straightforward wicked ones are [almost] to be honored, just like the virtuous!
Alas, the mind of the crooked-minded wicked is hard to grasp!
One thing is on the tongue, another in the throat, another on the lip.
We have set out among the wicked to acquire virtues —
this is like the farce of buying gems in a thieves' village!
Both grow, as if in rivalry, with a hundred-branched prosperity:
the sprout born from a seed, and the man born from a [noble] family.
The lowly, burned by the fierce fire of others' fame,
being unable to attain that station, therefore resort to slander.
That which, merely by being remembered, drives the virtuous to extreme anguish —
that very thing the wicked do laughingly, with utter contempt.
How can a person ignorant of the scriptures distinguish between virtue and vice?
Does a blind person have any authority in perceiving differences of form?
The wicked generally becomes conspicuous through harassing the virtuous;
if [<s>Rāhu</s>] had not swallowed the sun, who would know the son of <s>Siṃhikā</s>?
The wicked is constantly engaged, for the most part, in causing suffering to others;
since it must be done [in his view], he does not look for a reason.
By a little, he rises; by a little, he falls to the depths —
ah, how similar is the behavior of the tip of a balance-scale and that of the wicked!
Ah, how similar in nature are phlegm and the wicked person!
Angered by sweet things, pacified by bitter ones.
Just as a weary elephant-lord, seeking shade, takes shelter under a tree,

children.text: viśramya taṃ drumaṃ hanti tathā nīcaḥ svamāśrayam //
children.translated_text: and having rested, destroys that very tree — so does the base one [destroy] his own refuge.
The wicked person should be avoided even if adorned with learning;

children.text: maṇinā bhūṣitaḥ sarpo bhavetkiṃ na bhayaṃkaraḥ //
children.translated_text: is a serpent adorned with a gem any less fearsome?
Charm [is used] for [seducing] others' wives; wealth for tormenting the world;
power for the destruction of the virtuous — in the wicked, virtues are even more wicked.
For those who live only on the knowledge of how to harm others —
as for fishermen, so for the cunning — the collection of 'virtues' (threads) is but a net.
Even sweet words spoken by the wicked
cause me terror, like flowers blooming out of season.
The wicked one is not ashamed even of serpent-like crookedness,
which should be shunned by the virtuous;
the rogue considers his scheming, sorcerous intellect
to be cleverness itself.

children.text: vṛtiṃ svāṃ bahu manyate hṛdi śucaṃ dhattenukampoktibhir-
children.translated_text: The common man esteems his own conduct greatly, harbors grief in his heart at words of sympathy,
openly censures competence while praising himself, a man of limited intellect;
he speaks of reprehensible methods as stable, calls misfortune steady —

children.text: śrutvā duḥkhamaruṃtudāṃ vitanute pīḍāṃ janaḥ prākṛtaḥ //
children.translated_text: and upon hearing, he inflicts the agonizing pain of sorrow.

children.text: pākaścenna śubhasya medya tadasau prāgeva nādātkimu
children.translated_text: 'If this is not the ripening of [his] good fortune, why did he not give before?'

children.text: svārthaścenna mayāsya kiṃ na bhajate dīnānsvabandhūnayam /
children.translated_text: 'If this is not self-interest, why does he not attend to his own destitute kinsmen?'

children.text: matto randhrudṛśosya bhīryadi na tallubdhaḥ kimeṣa tyajed-
children.translated_text: 'If there is no fear of me discovering his weakness — then would this greedy one give it up?' —
thus, the base person, when given aid, generally rationalizes [it away] within.
His marvelous, irresistible valor in battle — by which <s>Indra</s> was humbled;
the open-palmed one (<s>Bali</s>) made the Lord of <s>Lakṣmī</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>) a recipient through his generosity;
sovereignty over seven worlds won by his own hand; fame that crossed the ocean —

children.text: sarvaṃ durjanasaṃgamena sahasā spaṣṭaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ baleḥ //
children.translated_text: all of <s>Bali</s>'s [glory] was suddenly and clearly destroyed by association with the wicked.

children.text: śamayati yaśaḥ kleśaṃ sūte diśatyaśivāṃ gatiṃ
children.translated_text: It destroys fame, begets suffering, leads to an inauspicious fate,
produces in people the weariness of anxiety, brings ridicule,

children.text: bhramayati matiṃ mānaṃ hanti kṣiṇoti ca jīvitaṃ
children.translated_text: confounds the intellect, slays honor, and diminishes life —
the company of the wicked destroys the entire family of auspicious things.
Study, which leads to the pacification of the ill-mannered and the ignorant,
only increases wickedness in one who is crooked by nature;
the gem-light on a serpent's hood may be able to cut through the darkness of those afraid of serpents,
but it only greatly increases [their] fear.
Even when honored, the wicked, who is dedicated to the world's misery,
causes terror at every encounter, like a house-snake.
From a man who has fallen from truth and <s>dharma</s>, as from an angry cobra,
even an atheist recoils — how much more the faithful!

children.text: yeṣāṃ prāṇivadhaḥ krīḍā narma marmacchido giraḥ /
children.translated_text: Those for whom killing creatures is sport, whose words pierce to the marrow,
whose business is the torment of others — they are the deaths of Death itself.
Alas, what great misery! How topsy-turvy is this world!
That by which the virtuous is dissatisfied, by that very thing the wicked is pleased.
The wicked do not so much desire to know the virtues of others
as those evil-minded ones desire to know [others'] lack of virtue.
A wicked person should be avoided by the wise, whether in friendship or in enmity;
a dog causes harm whether fawning or biting.
Nothing more laughable than this exists in the world:

children.text: yatra durjana ityāha durjanaḥ sajjanaṃ janam //
children.translated_text: that a wicked person calls a good person 'wicked.'
A virtuous person, even when not receiving injury from the wicked, should be content —

children.text: naiṣa lābho bhujaṃgena veṣṭito yanna daśyate //
children.translated_text: is it not a gain to be embraced by a serpent and not bitten?
Having gained power, the foolish one — stiff, perverse, and absolutely cruel —
this villain, having killed many good people, will [himself] perish.
What contest can there be between a self-respecting good person and a villain,
whose speech is frightening, whose ornament is the defamation of the good?
Thorns pierce the foot of one person with a single point;
villains, with a thousand points and from afar, destroy the life of all.
Having created the tip of the villain's tongue, which takes the life of all men,
why did <s>Prajāpati</s> (the Creator) needlessly create weapons, poison, and fire?
Just as the good person is always vigilant in helping others,
so the villain is constantly vigilant in harming others.
The lowly person fears the slanderer, who is expert at exposure;
but the dull-hearted one does not [fear] his own blameworthy deeds.
For the wicked one — whose anger-fire blazes in vain, who speaks harsh syllables —
there is no medicine other than silence.
The remedy for villains and thorns is twofold only:
either crushing the face with a shoe, or avoiding them from afar.
Even while alive, a good person cannot do what
a wicked one, when dead, would do — [namely,] the supreme benefit for others.
That which is most dear should be given to the virtuous, they say;
that is precisely why the villain bestows his faults upon the good.
A boil, a seedling of castor, fire, a mule, woodworms, and maggots,
and a person ungrateful by nature — they do not thrive without destroying their own shelter.

children.text: na vinā paravādena ramate durjano janaḥ /
children.translated_text: A wicked person takes no delight except in speaking ill of others;

children.text: śvā hi sarvarasānbhuktvā vināmedhyaṃ na tṛpyati //
children.translated_text: a dog, even after eating all other flavors, is not satisfied without filth.
Better a good person who is completely fruitless yet pleasant to serve,
than a villain who, like an arrow, is fruitful [in aim] yet life-destroying and sharp.
Sharp by nature, and even taking sides,
the villain — like an arrow released from a bowstring (<s>guṇa</s>/virtue) — who does he not pierce?
A wicked person cannot be made good even with effort;
who can make garlic fragrant, even with [culinary] refinement?
The lowly one, having risen, must inevitably take refuge in another;
he takes delight through [finding] a weakness — the example here is the waist-cloth.
In speaking ill of others, [the lowly is] ten-faced (<s>Rāvaṇa</s>); in spying others' weaknesses, thousand-eyed (<s>Indra</s>);
in stealing the livelihood of the virtuous, the lowly one is thousand-armed <s>Arjuna</s> (<s>Kārtavīrya</s>).
Those whose minds have been corrupted by the wicked have no trust even in the good;
a child scalded by milk-porridge blows even on yogurt before eating it.

children.text: ādau lajjayati kṛtaṃ madhye paribhavati riktamavasāne /
children.translated_text: At first it brings shame, in the middle it causes humiliation, and at the end it leaves one empty —
tell me, is there anything good in the company of a villain?
In villains — who see the vital points of others like divine seers, whose hostility is innately concealed,

children.text: kaḥ khalu khaleṣu śaṅkāṃ ślathayiṣyati dambhānirateṣu //
children.translated_text: who are devoted to hypocrisy — who indeed would relax his suspicion?
An ignorant person is easy to please; even easier is the specialist to please;
but a person made foolish by a smattering of knowledge — even <s>Brahmā</s> cannot satisfy him.

children.text: asthānābhiniveśī prāyo jaḍe eva bhavati no vidvān /
children.translated_text: Obstinate fixation in the wrong place is generally found only in the dull, not in the learned;
who other than a child would try to grasp the gleaming orb of the moon in a pot of water?

children.text: labdhodayopi hi khalaḥ prathamaṃ svajanaṃ nayati paritāpam /
children.translated_text: Even upon rising to power, the villain first brings torment upon his own people;
a fire, upon kindling, burns the wood of its own birthplace.
One with but a drop of learning generally displays his verbal power loudly;

children.text: sarvatra kunaṭa eva hi nāṭakamadhikaṃ viḍambayati //
children.translated_text: everywhere, it is the bad actor who most distorts the drama.

children.text: prakhalā eva guṇāvatāmākramya dhuraṃ puraḥ prakarṣanti /
children.translated_text: The brazen ones alone, mounting the yoke ahead of the virtuous, pull [the cart] forward;
it is grass and sticks that float on the surface of the ocean, not gems.

children.text: mahatāṃ yadeva mūrdhasu tadeva nīcāstṛṇāya manyante /
children.translated_text: What the great place upon their heads, the lowly consider as mere straw;
the wise bow before the <s>liṅga</s> (Śiva's emblem); the crow defecates upon it.
Even when dwelling together, the contact of the wicked [with the good] is like that of a lotus-leaf and water;
but even when living far apart, the affection of the virtuous arises like that of the night-lotus and the moon.
Even having adopted a perfectly pure livelihood, the wicked person torments others;
serpents, even though they feed on air, do not abandon the infliction of pain on others.
Whatever purpose an ignorant person accomplishes — that is a mere coincidence, like the crow and the palm-fruit;
by chance alone, the wood-worm too carves a letter in wood.
Generally, those of villainous nature do not serve a good purpose unless they are humiliated;
the <s>Aśoka</s> tree blooms more profusely when struck by the foot of a dancing woman.
The villain's skill in striking at another's vital points is not [seen] in [useful] work;
the power of poison in causing harm is not [seen] in rendering benefit.

children.text: atisatkṛtāapi śaṭhāḥ sahabhuvamujjhanti jātu na prakṛtim /
children.translated_text: Even when greatly honored, rogues never abandon their inborn nature;

children.text: śirasā mahāśvareṇāpi nanu dhṛto vakra eva śaśī //
children.translated_text: even when held upon the head by the great <s>Maheśvara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), the moon remains crooked.
Like the wind, this villainous person generally assumes the form of whatever he contacts;
but the virtuous, like the rays of the sun, remain unattached even in contact with the pure or impure.
Even penniless, the ignoble incites another to injure the world;
the whetstone sharpens the sword's edge, though itself unable to cut.
A person is keen at perceiving another's fault even from afar, but not his own even at close range;

children.text: svaṃ vraṇamakṣi na paśyati śaśini kalaṅkaṃ nirūpayati //
children.translated_text: one's own wound — the eye does not see; but it discerns the stain on the moon.
Those who wound the good alone reveal their [true] conduct particularly [toward] the virtuous;

children.text: vyādhā nighnanti mṛgānmṛtamapi na tu siṃhamādadate //
children.translated_text: hunters slay deer but do not dare even touch a dead lion.
The ignoble constantly torments the good even when they are unperturbed — this is the meaning;

children.text: kamalinyā kimiha kṛtaṃ himasya yattāṃ sadā dahati //
children.translated_text: what has the lotus done to the frost, that it always burns it?

children.text: svaguṇāniva paradoṣānvaktuṃ na satopi śakruvanti budhāḥ /
children.translated_text: The wise, even when virtuous, cannot speak of others' faults as if they were their own virtues;
but villains, even when lacking virtue, proclaim others' faults as if they were their own virtues.
That which even when done brings shame to the good person when mentioned by another —
that very thing the villain, without having done it, proclaims himself — shame on such pettiness!
The villain does not count even his own destruction as a cost, provided others suffer misfortune;
generally, at the battle-front, a headless trunk dances amid the destruction of thousands.

children.text: prakṛtikhalatvādasatāṃ doṣa iva guṇopi bādhate lokān /
children.translated_text: Due to the innate villainy of the wicked, even their virtue harms people, just like a fault;
the fragrance of poisonous flowers, though sweet, bewilders the mind.
The lowly one, upon rising to power, first dishonors his own master;
road-dust, upon first rising, covers the very one who raised it.
Though perfumed with musk, camphor, aloe, and sandalwood, garlic

children.text: na tyajati gandhamaśubhaṃ prakṛtimiva sahotthitāṃ nīcaḥ //
children.translated_text: does not abandon its foul smell — [just as] the lowly one does not [abandon] his innate nature.
Among the wicked, there is never the consideration: 'A kindness has been done to me by this friend';
fire, when it flares up, burns its own shelter along with the oblation.

children.text: upakṛtireva khalānāṃ doṣasya garīyaso bhavati hetuḥ /
children.translated_text: A kindness done to the wicked becomes the cause of a greater fault;
for diseases flare up with a regimen that is too agreeable — this is the meaning.

children.text: na paraṃ phalati hi kiṃcitkhala evānarthamāvahati yāvat /
children.translated_text: Nothing else brings as much misfortune as the villain himself;
the poison-tree immediately kills the one who takes shelter [under it] to relieve fatigue.
Even without self-interest, causing harm to others is the very addiction of the wicked;

children.text: aśanāyodanyā vā viramati phaṇino na dandaśataḥ //
children.translated_text: the serpent's biting does not cease from hunger, thirst, or [any other cause].
Though water and milk become mixed together, and though the minds of friends [appear to merge],
the power to separate [them again] belongs to swans and to villains.
Even a spike smeared with <s>hālāhala</s> (deadly poison) can be endured by the resolute when it slips [in];
but not the false, harsh words of a villain who is angry without cause.
Deer, fish, and good people — sustaining themselves contentedly on grass, water, and [simple pleasures] —
hunters, fishermen, and slanderers are their causeless enemies in the world.
Vastly large at the beginning, extremely thin at the end, causing division, soiled —
like the horn of a buffalo: crooked and fearsome — such is the love of a villain.
It renders the worthy unworthy, it burns virtues, it swiftly destroys affection,
it bestows impurity upon the pure — the friendship of a villain is like a lamp-flame.
Upon whom has the villain not foisted faults?
Or whose virtues has he not forcibly stolen?
Yet he himself is never parted from his faults,
nor is he touched by even a single virtue — how wondrous!
That he cannot be won over even when propitiated in many ways —
what wonder is there in that?
But this is an unprecedented marvel of nature:
that when served, he assumes enmity.
A learned person, upon receiving a rebuke, turns away from faults
and feels remorse;
but the wicked person, thinking 'My fault is now known in all ways,'
proceeds to commit even greater wickedness.
Thus indeed, life is impossible alongside the villain —
what then to say of a villain who is the king's favorite?
A forest fire is already unbearable by itself;
how much more so when driven by a powerful wind!
The nectar was not drunk by the gods from the ocean,
nor was the terrible <s>hālāhala</s> (poison) [drunk] by <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>) —
by the decree [of fate], both have been placed in the villain's speech:
the one externally, the other internally.
He who becomes angry on account of a specific cause
will surely be appeased when that cause is removed;
but he whose mind harbors causeless hatred —
how can another ever satisfy him?
What is said outwardly is one thing;
what flashes in the heart is quite another —
this is the conduct of the wicked, destroying trust,
like the reflection of milk in front [of water].
Where is the slanderer's progress checked?
He bites what is seen and what is heard;
this is extremely difficult [to guard against] — with eyes that see without exception,
and with ears that are [themselves] poison-eyed.
Let fools go with hundreds of elephants and horses;
let the learned, though penniless, go on foot —
a flock of crows perched on a mountain-peak
does not mingle with the royal swans on the sandbank.
He shames with sweet words, shows regard while making a fool of [you],
and while elevating, diminishes — a foolish friend should be avoided in every way.
This company of the virtuous does not conceal even a manifest fault,
being devoted to even a trace of virtue;
but the era of the slanderous dogs passes
in exceedingly harsh anger, even without [anyone's] faults.
When he quarrels, fame is destroyed;
when he makes friendship, virtues are corrupted —
the discerning one, considering the situation in both cases,
treats the common person with contempt.
Whether favored, nurtured by a hundred good deeds,
embraced, or protected through a hundred adversities —
the wicked person, due to his evil nature, never inspires trust,
like a serpent sleeping in one's lap.
He snarls harshly, becomes angry without cause,
contaminates by his touch, and bars entry;
he bites shamefully and is never satisfied —

children.text: kauleyakasya ca khalasya ca ko viśeṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: what is the difference between a household dog and a villain?
Whether struck by a foot or hit hard with a stick,

children.text: yaṃ daṃṣṭrayā daśati taṃ kila hanti sarpaḥ /
children.translated_text: a serpent bites that person and kills him;
but the slanderer, another with the nature of a serpent,
touches one person's ear and destroys another from the root.
That [learning] by which the spread of the darkness of arrogance
in one who has unceasingly obtained a livelihood should properly be checked —
some, relying on that very learning in the world,
extend their ego — ah, a hundredfold-branching blindness!
O <s>Kālakūṭa</s> (deadly poison), surely this progression of your abode
has been directed to ever-higher stations!
Formerly in the heart of the ocean, then on the throat of <s>Vṛṣalakṣmaṇa</s> (<s>Śiva</s>),
and now you dwell in the speech of villains.
Generally, the villain — impure by nature — while standing near the great,
inflicts harm upon the common people;
even [a fire] that brings comfort to the whole world when it is cold —
when smoke persists, fire cannot be enjoyed in comfort. //
Smoke, somehow reaching the station of a cloud,
with its rains quenches the fire's blaze.
One of impure nature, having by fate attained greatness,
generally scorns his own kinfolk. //
Of the wicked one — elated, unbridled,
who has forgotten his former base way of life,
who has obtained wealth by fate, who hates virtue —
by whom within his reach can comfort be had? //
It is no wonder now — by the conjunction of wretched fate —
that the base person stands in a lofty position, though not great of soul.
Even when mixed with a hundred stains of the street's filth,
rubbish rises on top — but it does not become a treasure. //
One may forcibly extract a gem from between the fangs of a crocodile's jaws,
one may cross the ocean turbulent with surging waves,
one may wear upon the head an enraged serpent as though it were a flower —
but one cannot win over the mind of a fool deeply set in his ways. //
One might extract oil from sand by pressing with effort,
one might, tormented by thirst, drink water from a mirage,
one might someday obtain the horn of a roaming hare —
but one cannot win over the mind of a fool deeply set in his ways. //
Weeping in the wilderness, massaging a corpse,
planting a lotus on dry land, watering a salt flat for long,
straightening a dog's tail, whispering into a deaf man's ear,
adorning the face of a blind man — such is nourishing the ignorant. //
A bull was milked in vain; a eunuch was long embraced [thinking him] a woman
endowed with grace and heavy breasts.
Hope for a cat's-eye gem was placed in a glittering piece of glass —
[such was] my foolishness in bowing to you, O wretched one, ignorant of merit! //
The clipping of its own wings, or the loss of its proper fruit,
or the shattering of its own body, or a fall into filth, or destruction —
an arrow suffers all these even while resting on the path of the bowstring.
From the embrace of the crooked by the straight, misfortune clearly arises. //
It is the power of virtues that misfortunes attach themselves to these [virtuous ones].
'My satisfaction [comes from the fact] that Fate did not bring about their union [with me]' —
seeing a person of merit dejected by misfortune, the meritless one
surely celebrates a festival of great prosperity in his own house. //
Seeing himself without merit, he desires others [to be] likewise.
If this does not bear fruit, he laments: 'There are no meritorious people here!'
He then undertakes to wipe out, curse, or insult [the virtuous] —
ah, how delightful is the innate desire of the base to conquer the virtuous! //

children.text: yadi paraguṇā na kṣamyante yatasva tadarjane
children.translated_text: If you cannot tolerate the virtues of others, strive to acquire them.
Another's fame cannot be wiped away by the pretense of censure.
And if you do not desist, your wishes being engaged in envy and hatred,
you will grow weary trying to ward off the sun's rays with hand-held parasols. //
In the close association of gem and serpent, born together since birth,
the gem does not take on the serpent's faults, nor the serpent the gem's qualities.

children.text: asādhuḥ sādhurvā bhavati nanu jātyaiva puruṣo
children.translated_text: A man is base or noble indeed by birth itself;
neither wickedness nor goodness arises from anyone's association. //
Poison cannot be made into nectar, even by a hundred efforts.

children.text: tyajati kaṭutāṃ na svāṃ nimbaḥ sthitopi payohrade /
children.translated_text: The neem tree does not abandon its bitterness even when standing in a lake of milk.
The wicked person does not speak the noble speech cultivated by virtue —
no matter how long iron is blown upon in the forge, how can it assume the form of gold? //
Better to place one's hands in the mouth of a serpent enraged with fury;
better to drink poison and sleep in the abode of Death;
better to hurl oneself from the summit of a great mountain and be shattered a hundredfold —
than to have one's welfare served by wealth obtained from the wicked. //

children.text: varṇasthaṃ gurulāghavaṃ na gaṇathatyāśaṅkate na kvacid-
children.translated_text: He does not count propriety of syllables, never suspects [error] anywhere

children.text: rūpaṃ naiva parīkṣate na puruṣaṃ vṛtteṣu vārtā kutaḥ /
children.translated_text: regarding form, does not examine the person — what talk of conduct?
The wretch neither fears great infamy nor [cares about] mispronunciations —
Death, the foolish poet, the rogue, the bad king, and the thief are equal in their workings. //
A lion took the dear life of <s>Pāṇini</s>, the maker of grammar;
an elephant swiftly gored the sage <s>Jaimini</s>, the author of <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>;
a crocodile killed <s>Piṅgala</s>, the treasury of prosodic knowledge, at the water's edge —
what gain have beasts, filled with excessive anger and struck by ignorance, from virtues? //
He reviles the venerable, mocks the distressed, oppresses kinsmen,
hates the brave, insults the fallen in fortune, commands dependents,
reveals secrets, zealously fosters enmity,
quickly utters the unspeakable, abandons virtues, and seizes faults — such is the rogue. //
He laughs and exults with glee at others' intense suffering;
he stumbles and falls from delusion at the slightest affliction of his own.

children.text: nadati vadati nindyaṃ mānināṃ kiṃ ca nīcaḥ
children.translated_text: The base one roars and speaks what is censurable about the proud;
hearing even a little harsh speech, he sets out to kill. //
If you will be devoted to the company of the virtuous, you will flourish, you will flourish!
But if [you linger] at the gatherings of the wicked, you will fall, you will fall! //
They whisper in the ear what drums have announced throughout the kingdom;
they declare piteously, with bowed bodies, what [should cause] shame.
They praise what even an enemy proclaims — the fierce [deed] that does not cut to the core.
Certain ones — treasuries of foolishness, worthy of being decried — are the entertainers of kings! //
The jester [is glorious] on the stage of dance; the rag-poet in the lanes of flattering tales;
the gossip in his own courtyard; clearly, the mouse in the mountain-cave.
The rogue, with the heroism of a glutton, plunges into boldness in the king's palace.
Wondrous — they achieve the weight of a tortoise drawn from a lake, but elsewhere [they are nothing]! //

children.text: jāḍyaṃ hrīmati gaṇyate vratarucau dambhaḥ śucau kaitavaṃ
children.translated_text: In one who is modest, dullness is reckoned; in one fond of vows, hypocrisy; in the pure, deceit;

children.text: śūre nirghṛṇatā ṛjau vimatitā dainyaṃ priyālāpini /
children.translated_text: in the brave, cruelty; in the straightforward, folly; in the sweet-spoken, wretchedness;
in the spirited, arrogance; in the eloquent, garrulousness; in the steadfast, incapacity —

children.text: tatko nāma guṇo bhavedguṇavatāṃ yo durjanairnāṅkitaḥ //
children.translated_text: what quality indeed could there be of the virtuous that is not branded by the wicked? //
The mouse weighs Mount <s>Kailāsa</s>; the crow, craving <s>Garuḍa</s>'s flesh;
the mongoose shakes the base of its tail, wishing to kill the serpent <s>Takṣaka</s>;
the frog wishes to cross to the other shore of the ocean, vast devourer, [carrying] even a serpent —

children.text: prāyeṇāsannapātaḥ smarati samucitaṃ karma na kṣudrakarmā //
children.translated_text: generally, the small-minded one, near to his fall, remembers [only] the deed befitting [his delusion]. //
A particle of no-virtue and a heap of virtues — both, by fate, fall into the mouth of the rogue.
One spreads like oil upon water; the other congeals like ghee. //
Are riches a refuge that those who have recourse to them are protected? Do they kill like poison?

children.text: na tyajyante na bhujyante kṛpaṇena dhanāni yat //
children.translated_text: Since by the miser they are neither given away nor enjoyed — //

children.text: kṛpaṇena samo dātā na bhūto na bhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: There has never been nor will there be a giver equal to the miser,
who gives his wealth to others without even touching it! //
The misfortune that is new for the enjoyer and the generous at the loss of wealth —
that very [misfortune] has already been attained by the miser long before, through the impairment of his judgment. //
If rich men are [called] 'rich' by wealth devoid of generosity and enjoyment,

children.text: bhavāmaḥ kiṃ na tenaiva dhanena dhanino vayam //
children.translated_text: then why are we not rich by that same wealth? //
If one delights in wealth buried in the middle of the house,

children.text: sa tu tenānusāreṇa ramate kiṃ na meruṇā //
children.translated_text: then by that same logic, does he not delight in Mount <s>Meru</s>? //
What would a hungry parrot do with a <s>Kiṃśuka</s> (flame-of-the-forest) tree, even when in fruit?
What would dependents do with a rich man who does not give? //
If wealth that is barren of giving and enjoyment, that is not shared with friends,

children.text: puṃsāṃ yadi hi sā lakṣmīralakṣmīḥ katama bhavet //
children.translated_text: is [called] prosperity (<s>Lakṣmī</s>) of men — then what would misfortune (<s>Alakṣmī</s>) be? //
The wealth of those who hoard excessively becomes the occasion for others.
It is collected with effort by some, and the honey is drunk by others. //
What you give to the worthy, and what you eat day by day —

children.text: tatte vittamahaṃ manye śeṣaṃ kasyāpi rakṣasi //
children.translated_text: that I consider your true wealth; the rest you are guarding for someone else. //
Wealth in a man who is promiscuous in his affections to others is merely a mockery.
What splendor would the fashioning of an armlet produce on a [person's deformed] stump? //
He who, having performed a favor, desires reciprocation from [the recipient] —
that wretched one, enslaved by craving, licks up even what has been vomited. //

children.text: dānaṃ bhogo nāśastisro gatayo bhavanti vittasya /
children.translated_text: Giving, enjoyment, and destruction — these are the three courses of wealth.

children.text: yo na dadāti na bhuṅkte tasya tṛtīyā gatirnāśaḥ //
children.translated_text: He who neither gives nor enjoys — for him, the third course is destruction. //

children.text: dānaṃ bhogaṃ ca vinā dhanasattāmātrakeṇa ceddhaninaḥ /
children.translated_text: If rich men [are considered rich] merely by the existence of wealth, without giving or enjoyment,

children.text: vayamapi kimiti na dhaninistiṣṭhati naḥ kāñcano meruḥ //
children.translated_text: then why are we not rich? The golden <s>Meru</s> stands [available] to us! //
The wealthy who neither give nor enjoy are counted at the head of the greatly destitute.

children.text: hanti na yataḥ pipāsāmataḥ samudropi marureva //
children.translated_text: Because it does not quench thirst, even the ocean is [merely] a desert. //
Employed by the virtuous, coming and going day after day, completely disgusted —
riches, upon reaching the proximity of the miserly, seem to fall asleep. //
For those who are reluctant to enjoy and devoted to hoarding wealth,
riches dwell in their house like a daughter-jewel — for the sake of another. //

children.text: te mūrkhatarā loke yeṣāṃ dhanamasti nāsti ca tyāgaḥ /
children.translated_text: The most foolish in the world are those who have wealth but have no generosity.
They experience only the sorrows of acquisition, protection, and the grief of parting. //
There are certain exceedingly clever ones who enjoy even the fortunes of the miserly.
The waters of the ocean constantly dissolve into the submarine fire. //

children.text: prāptānapi na labhante bhogānbhoktuṃ svakarmabhiḥ kṛpaṇāḥ /
children.translated_text: Misers cannot enjoy the pleasures obtained, due to their own <s>karma</s>.

children.text: mukharogaḥ kila bhavati drākṣāpāke balibhujāṃ hi //
children.translated_text: Indeed, mouth-disease afflicts the crows when grapes ripen! //
Riches do not wish to depart from the miser's hand,
like drops of oil from dust.
By fate, when they do wish to go forth from the spender,
they desire to leave along with his very life-breaths. //
The hoarded [wealth] is not employed in sacrifices;
when asked for, it is not given to the meritorious.
That wealth guarded by the miser
goes to the houses of thieves, kings, or fire. //
Better these trees roaming in the forest,
whose fruit-wealth is carried away by flocks of birds,
than the wealthy misers, whose ways are those
of serpents sitting upon hoarded gems! //
Well-hidden, guarded as if alive,
with restraints imposed even upon one's own body —
following your path through subsequent lives,
the treacherous riches did not complete even five steps. //
Ah, the great cleverness of riches
comfortably dwelling in the miser's house!
They reach neither the state of being given nor that of being enjoyed,
yet they manifest some other supreme contentment. //
Thirst is not quenched within by the mixing of the salt-water of wealth;
the body is wasted in shade through the long, tasteless, harsh eating;
sleeplessness, weak digestion, fear of king, water, thief, and fire —
the suffering of the miserly is clearly greater than the suffering of the poor. //
Surpassing in each [quality] individually, connoisseurs singularly skilled in knowing others' merits,
these wealthy ones are fierce in the practice of mastery in all arts —
yet even they tremble at hearing the pleasant words of praise — ah!

children.text: dhūte mūrdhani kuṇḍale kaṣaṇataḥ kṣīṇe bhavetāmiti //
children.translated_text: 'If the head is shaken [in appreciation], the earrings may diminish from the friction!' //
He does not show affection to a friend, out of apprehension of expenditure of goods;
afraid — from fear of the cause of reciprocal service — he is not drawn in by attentions.
He speaks falsely, from fear of being asked for wealth; he is not pleased even by praise.
The wretched miser, terrified by the prospect of expense of fortune — how does he even breathe? //

children.text: matvā sāraṃ guṇānāṃ śirasi yadi śaśī sthāpito daivayogā-
children.translated_text: If the moon was placed upon the head [of <s>Śiva</s>] for being deemed the essence of virtues,

children.text: dīśena kṣīṇabimbaṃ sakalamupacayaṃ kiṃ na nītaḥ kṣaṇena /
children.translated_text: then, by a twist of fate, with its orb waning — why was it not wholly augmented by the Lord in an instant?
Thus falsely proclaiming their generosity toward the meritorious, for the sake of worldly reputation,
the rich, with minds terrified by the expenditure of wealth, bestow honor that is empty of substance. //
The entire sphere of the universe — is it cause for greed to the noble-minded?
By the leaping of small fish, agitation is never born in the ocean. //
Those of unbridled spirit do not set foot on anything small,
whose aspirations are limitless even at the acquisition of the world. //
For men of lofty mind, these two [alone] bring happiness:
either the cessation of all attachment, or the most extensive splendor. //

children.text: ayaṃ bandhuḥ paro veti gaṇanā laghucetasām /
children.translated_text: 'This one is a kinsman, that one is a stranger' — such reckoning belongs to the petty-minded.
For those of noble mind, the entire earth is [their] family. //
Old age, death, destitution, diseases — let these assail —

children.text: janmaiva kiṃ na dhīrasya bhūyo bhūyastrapākaram //
children.translated_text: Is not the very birth of a steadfast one a cause of repeated shame? //

children.text: parivartini saṃsāre mṛtaḥ ko vā na jāyate /
children.translated_text: In the revolving cycle of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), who that has died is not born again?

children.text: sa jāto yena jātena yāti vaṃśaḥ samunnatim //
children.translated_text: He alone is [truly] born by whose birth the lineage rises to eminence. //

children.text: api nāma sa dṛśyeta puruṣātiśayo bhuvi /
children.translated_text: If only that extraordinary man could be seen upon the earth,
by whom the wealthy, with faces swollen with pride, were not even glanced at! //

children.text: pṛthvī pṛthvī guṇā mānyāḥ santi bhūpā vivekinaḥ /
children.translated_text: On this broad earth, virtues are honored — there are kings who are discerning.
Why then do those of lofty intellect fall into the state of humiliation? //
It is fitting for one who has never seen the aversion of a face, for the blind one, to beg.
Alas, what great misery — even one who has eyes begs! //
The burning heat of the fire of poverty is quenched by the water of contentment.
Who can see the inner burning caused by the thwarting of a beggar's hopes? //
He alone is exalted, replete with the fullness of abundant virtues,
in whom the three worlds find cause for desire — not in one who merely possesses wealth. //

children.text: vidyayaiva mado yeṣāṃ kārpaṇyaṃ ca dhane sati /
children.translated_text: Those whose intoxication is from learning alone, and who feel wretchedness even when wealth is present —
for those cursed by fate, fire has arisen from water! //

children.text: kiṃ tayā kriyate lakṣmyā yā vadhūriva kevalā /
children.translated_text: What use is that <s>Lakṣmī</s> (wealth/goddess of fortune) who is like a chaste wife, exclusive to one alone?

children.text: yā na veśyeva sāmānyā pathikairapi bhujyate //
children.translated_text: She who, like a courtesan, is shared commonly and enjoyed even by wayfarers! //

children.text: tyāgo guṇo vittavatāṃ vittaṃ tyāgavatāṃ guṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: Generosity is the virtue of the wealthy; wealth is the virtue of the generous.
But when separated from each other, both wealth and generosity are a mockery. //
The noble-minded have a twofold course, like a cluster of flowers:

children.text: mūrdhni vā sarvalokasya śīryate vana eva vā //
children.translated_text: either upon the head of all people, or withering away in the forest itself. //

children.text: nṛṇāṃ dhuri sa evaiko yaḥ kaścittyāgapāṇinā /
children.translated_text: Among men, he alone stands foremost — whoever he may be — who with the hand of generosity
wipes clean the faces of supplicants, gray with the dust of entreaty. //
Blessed are those whose desires are fulfilled by merely perceiving the expression [of the petitioner],

children.text: dhanyāste ye na śṛṇvanti dīnāḥ praṇayināṃ giraḥ //
children.translated_text: who do not [need to] hear the pitiable words of their dependents. //
Intellect devoid of <s>sattva</s> (courage/inner strength) is considered mere femininity.
And <s>sattva</s> endowed with dishonesty — that is bestiality, not manliness. //
The noble-minded willingly abandon even their beloved life-breaths,
but they do not desire even a great favor from their enemies. //
I consider this nature of the ignoble most astonishing:
that even when being helped, he neither rejoices nor melts [with gratitude]. //
The mind of one who reciprocates a previously rendered service feels ashamed even before acting.
But one who returns a favor [unsolicited] to a benefactor — that [reciprocity] is greater than death! //
Even one who reciprocates abundantly does not become equal to the original benefactor.
For one acts in return for what was done, while the other acts without any cause at all. //

children.text: jīvañjīvayati hi yo jñātijanaṃ parijanaṃ ca suhṛdaśca /
children.translated_text: He who, while living, sustains his kinsmen, dependents, and friends —
for him the glory of the household is fruitful; he has attained wealth that is not merely parasitically enjoyed. //
Even the rain-cloud, though it gives only water, becomes dear to all the world.
The sun, though always extending its rays, becomes unpleasant to the eyes. //

children.text: nāptaṃ yatkenacidapi manorathā api yato nivartante /
children.translated_text: That which has not been attained by anyone, from which even desires turn back —
even if that is not obtained otherwise, for the noble-minded, what use is the fruit of mere self-regard? //
The accomplishment or failure of undertakings occurs by the decree of fate.
Engagement or withdrawal from proper and improper action — that is within my control. //

children.text: kalpasthāyi na jīvitamaiścaryaṃ nāpyate ca yadabhimatam /
children.translated_text: Life does not last an aeon, nor is desired glory attained.
Yet the world still commits wrong deeds — with what purpose in mind? //
Without abundance of wealth as a cause, someone is by nature open-handed.
In the rainy season, is the cloud's prosperity greater than the ocean's? //
If this <s>Śrī</s> (wealth/fortune) was produced by oneself, then she is a daughter;

children.text: tātena vā yadi tadā bhaginī khalu śrīḥ /
children.translated_text: or if by one's father, then she is surely a sister.
If she consorts with another, then she is another's wife —
therefore the wise are those whose minds are set on renunciation. //
The toil born of earning wealth,
even when fruitful, is joyless for this person.
Earning wealth is for self-satisfaction,
but the supreme [goal] is to earn virtues and to win over others. //
That man who praises another man
while boon-granting deities exist,
foolish in mind, craving a mere morsel of wealth —
him I consider the cruelest wretch today. //
Just as the body, indeed, when deprived of life,
appears like [a piece of] wood,
so too I understand even a life bereft of shame
to be empty of any extraordinary spark. //
Even existing, where can the virtuous radiate their brilliance?

children.text: kva nojjvalantu kva nu na prathantām /
children.translated_text: Where can they not shine? Where can they not spread their fame?
But they have been confined by <s>Brahmā</s> (the Creator) himself,
within the shell of the cosmic egg, like lamps inside a pot! //
Even when one of steadfast resolve is humiliated,
the quality of <s>sattva</s> (inner strength) cannot be wiped away.
Even when fire is held facing downward,
its flames never go downward. //
That one who is born shall not perish — this is illogical.
The very fact of origination is inevitably the cause of destruction.
Since the calamity of death is equal for all,
death is preferable for one whose mind is devoted to the welfare of others. //
On this immeasurably vast path, even these qualities —

children.text: ta evāmī dvitrā jaraṭhajaraṭhā yānti gaṇanām /
children.translated_text: just those same two or three, exceedingly ancient — come to be counted.

children.text: aho grāmyo lokaḥ sa na paramamībhiḥ kṛtadhṛtiḥ
children.translated_text: Alas, the vulgar world, having relied upon these mere trifles,
stands frozen with pride, as if considering this entire [world] a blade of grass! //
The noble-minded do not harbor anguish within themselves merely by the reflection of their own minds,

children.text: na bibhrati manāsvino yadamunā na tāvatkṣatiḥ /
children.translated_text: since thereby no real harm befalls them.
But those who day and night seek to triumph
by pandering to another's mind — what a pitiable state! //
The world was created long ago by certain others of expansive heart;
sustained by some, and conquered and given away by yet others as if it were a blade of grass.
Here, indeed, other bold ones enjoy the fourteen worlds —
what is this fever of pride in men who are lords of but a few cities? //

children.text: abhuktāyāṃ yasyāṃ kṣaṇamapi na yātaṃ nṛpaśatair-
children.translated_text: Of that earth which has not been left unenjoyed even for a moment by hundreds of kings,

children.text: bhuvastasyā lābhe ka iva bahumānaḥ kṣitibhujām /
children.translated_text: what great esteem can kings have in gaining her?
Yet even over a fraction of a fraction, over a mere particle of that portion,

children.text: viṣāde kartavye vidadhati jaḍāḥ pratyuta mudam //
children.translated_text: the foolish, when there is cause for sorrow, feel joy instead! //
O heart, striving in manifold ways day after day to win the favor of others,

children.text: prasādaṃ kiṃ netuṃ viśāsi hṛdaya kleśakalilam /
children.translated_text: why do you enter this thicket of affliction?
When you yourself are serene, possessing the self-arisen quality of a wish-fulfilling gem,

children.text: viviktaḥ saṃkalpaḥ kimabhilaṣitaṃ puṣyati na te //
children.translated_text: does not every wish flourish in solitary resolve? //
The steadfast one, even without wealth, attains the height of great esteem,
while the miser, even embraced by wealth, reaches the state of contempt.
The natural radiance born of an assemblage of virtues, vast and inherent,

children.text: dyutiṃ saiṃhīṃ na śvā dhṛtakanakamālopi labhate //
children.translated_text: the leonine splendor — a dog does not obtain it, even if adorned with a golden necklace. //

children.text: bhujyante svagṛhasthitā iva sukhaṃ yasyāthibhiḥ saṃpadaḥ
children.translated_text: He whose possessions are happily enjoyed by guests as if they were in their own homes,

children.text: paṭvī yasya matistamaḥprahataye dvāveva tau prāṇitaḥ /
children.translated_text: and he whose sharp intellect dispels darkness — these two alone have truly lived.
But he who feeds only himself, though elevated in fortune yet deficient in learning —
his existence is truly non-existence, like a figure painted on a gemstone, merely holding a form. //
The earth serves as support, space serves to provide expanse, and also sky for viewing;
the sun serves to establish its own greatness — and there are certain other qualities.
In this group of benefactors, ever supreme and most difficult to abandon,
how can the minds of the great-souled abandon the stain of shame at helplessness? //
That [wealth] which is never enjoyed at one's own pleasure by teachers, servants, kinsmen, and good people,

children.text: paśyanti spṛhayālavo na ripavo yāṃ vikramāsāditām /
children.translated_text: which enemies, though envious, cannot see — [wealth] acquired by valor —

children.text: yasyāḥ sādhuparikṣayeṇa suhṛdāṃ nāśena vā saṃbhavo
children.translated_text: whose accumulation comes through the expenditure of the good and the destruction of friends —

children.text: no saṃpadvipadeva sā guṇavatāṃ prītistayā kīdṛśī //
children.translated_text: such prosperity is no prosperity but calamity! What delight can the virtuous have in it? //
If misfortunes befall those who do not abandon the righteous path, through fate, let them come —
like those of mighty <s>Bali</s>, the primeval one, who himself offered up the earth.
Like <s>Indra</s>, through many extremely censurable, reprehensible deeds —
may even lordship over the gods not be mine, if it becomes a cause of shame! //
The bed is green grass, the seat a clean stone, the dwelling beneath the trees,

children.text: śītaṃ nirjharavāri pānamaśanaṃ kandāḥ sahāyā mṛgāḥ /
children.translated_text: the drink is cool waterfall water, the food is roots, the companions are deer.
Thus in the forest, where all desired things are obtained unasked, there is but this one flaw:
one stays fruitlessly, unable to serve others' purposes, among those whose efforts to help are barren. //
The departure from one's homeland is only for the lowly —
for the learned, there is no heedlessness.
Gems that have left their place reach
the heads of kings; frogs [merely reach] the mouths of crows. //
Heroes, accomplished scholars, and beautiful women —

children.text: yatra yatra gamiṣyanti tatra tatra kṛtālayāḥ //
children.translated_text: wherever they go, there they make their home. //

children.text: rudrodriṃ jaladhiṃ harirdiviṣado dūraṃ vihāyaḥ śritā
children.translated_text: <s>Rudra</s> has resorted to a mountain, <s>Hari</s> to the ocean, the gods to the distant sky;

children.text: bhogīndrāḥ prabalā api prathamataḥ pātālamūle sthitāḥ /
children.translated_text: the mighty serpent lords dwell first in the netherworld.
<s>Lakṣmī</s>, dwelling in lotuses, is hidden in the lotus-grove, as if out of fear of the throng of supplicants.
In the <s>Kali Yuga</s> (age of strife), only the virtuous are devoted to uplifting the wretched. //
The lowly do not even begin, out of fear of obstacles.
The middling begin but desist when struck by obstacles.
Even when beset by obstacles multiplied a thousandfold,
those of the highest quality do not abandon what they have undertaken. //
He whose virtues do not blossom even as his rays spread forth —
how does this moon, the repository of blemishes, possess perpetual fullness? //
As it wanes, the moon draws closer [to the sun]; when full, it moves very far away.
It is fitting that the moon is always tainted, given its conduct toward its friend [the sun]. //
How is that sun, the treasure-house of radiance, not ashamed?
Having reached [merely] a fragment of the cosmic egg, he stretches out his feet! //
Only the rising of the sun is praiseworthy — who cares about the rising of others?

children.text: na tamāṃsi na tejāṃsi yasminnabhyudite sati //
children.translated_text: For when he has risen, neither darkness nor [rival] lights exist. //
Is not this alone sufficient — the loveliness of the one marked with a hare (the moon)?
That even a lotus, though greatly scorched [by the sun], has placed its trust in him! //
By the sun, hanging low in the southern direction, stretching out its rays —
not only has the sun itself been diminished, but the day too has been made short. //

children.text: vartate yena pātaṅgiḥ ṣaṇmāsāndvau ca vatsarau /
children.translated_text: The zodiac sign in which the sun remains for six months and two years,

children.text: rāśiḥ sa eva candrasya na yāti divasatrayam //
children.translated_text: that same sign the moon does not traverse in even three days! //
Even though <s>Soma</s> (the moon) is borne upon the head by <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) himself,

children.text: tathāpi kṛśatāṃ dhatte kaṣṭaḥ khalu parāśrayaḥ // Qsv0552-3 pa. pājakasya
children.translated_text: still he assumes waning form — dependence on another is truly wretched indeed! //
Let it fall into water, let it go to the ends of the earth,

children.text: viśatu vahnimatho vrajatu kṣitim kathaṃ sa dantarahitaḥ sūryaḥ sūribhirucyate /
children.translated_text: let it enter fire or descend below the ground — How can the toothless sun be called wise by the learned? He who, having devoured the sign of <s>Mīna</s> (Pisces), is ready to devour <s>Meṣa</s> (Aries)! //

children.text: yo mīnarāśiṃ bhuktvaiva meṣaṃ bhoktuṃ samudyataḥ //
children.translated_text: He who, having devoured the sign of <s>Mīna</s> (Pisces), is about to devour <s>Meṣa</s> (Aries)! //
Let it fall into water, let it go to the ends of the earth,
let it enter fire or descend below the ground.
What diminishment is there of this sun, of boundless glory,
in its qualities that cause wonder to the entire world? //
The moon's radiance is magnified only so long
as it does not approach the orb of the sharp-rayed [sun].
But when that repository of all splendor rises,
what difference is there between the moon and a fragment of white cloud? //
Those of good conduct, who discriminate between right and wrong —
see what sort of character they attribute to this [moon]!
Whatever the eighty-four and others say about it —
if that is accepted, then the day-maker (sun) has accomplished [its purpose]. //
There is a single, nectar-filled, utterly priceless
digit of the moon, by which alone
the Supreme Lord, the knower of virtues, placed it
as a crest-jewel — he did not count its blemish as a fault. //
These many great luminaries arise,
and the moon too is sufficient for adorning the orb of the world.
But except for the sun, none other rises or sets
such that by its rising there is day, and by its setting there is night. //
He who does not cease delighting the world even as he wanes repeatedly —
indeed, had he remained in heaven, a new day would never have come about.
See, friend, what fate is like — even he, somehow, merely to sustain himself,

children.text: vyagraḥ kālaṃ gamayati sakhe sopyayaṃ paśya candraḥ //
children.translated_text: passes his time anxiously — look at this moon! //
The waning moon enters the orb of the sun month after month,
gaining some small digit, following from far, far away.
When somehow full, he rises in rivalry with the sun —
the dull one neither ceases from malice nor desists from wretchedness! //
Having placed his foot upon the summit of the great mountain <s>Sumeru</s>,

children.text: krāntaṃ yena kṣapitatamasā madhyamaṃ dhāma viṣṇoḥ /
children.translated_text: having traversed, with darkness dispelled, the middle realm of <s>Viṣṇu</s>,
this very moon falls from the sky with but a few remaining rays —
The ascent of the great is lofty, but ends in a fall. // Of <s>Kalaśakasa</s>:

children.text: pātaḥ pūṣṇo bhavati mahate nopatāpāya yasmāt-
children.translated_text: The fall of <s>Pūṣan</s> (the Sun) does not cause great distress, because —

children.text: kālenāstaṃ ka iva na gatā yānti yāsyanti cānye kva tattejastādṛgjvalanamahaso nāśapiśunaṃ
children.translated_text: who has not set in time? Others have gone and will go. Where is that brilliance of such blazing splendor, what sign of destruction?
Where is that defeat, from the utterly dissimilar head of <s>Rāhu</s>?
This is fitting by the conjunction of fate; but what causes anguish is that
the shameless one, even [departing] from [his] friend, still roams in the sky. //

children.text: pātaḥ pūṣṇo bhavati mahate nopatāpāya yasmāt-
children.translated_text: The fall of <s>Pūṣan</s> (the Sun) does not cause great distress, because —

children.text: kālenāstaṃ ka iva na gatā yānti yāsyanti cānye /
children.translated_text: who has not set in time? Others have gone and will go.
But this much causes anguish: that by the darkness excluded from light,
in that very great sky of [its] nature, [darkness] has found its opportunity. //
From creation onward, day after day, she who was nourished and awakened with hundreds of essences —

children.text: kalpāntāvasaretha saiva pṛthivī svaireva dagdhā karaiḥ /
children.translated_text: that very earth, at the occasion of the end of the <s>kalpa</s> (cosmic age), is burned by [his] rays at will.
Having thus done some deed of destiny, confused between before and after,
alas! Even the fierce-rayed <s>Tigmāṃśu</s> (Sun), his rays spent at the end of the day, has set. //
By whom, having churned away the darknesses — dense as flesh — the entire world
was truly made to have sight by this fierce-rayed god.
When that <s>Vivasvat</s> (Sun) has set, how cruel are the wicked people,
who take courage in the light of a crescent of the moon, or of a lamp! //
First, <s>Umāpati</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) is pitiable, who by his power equally bears upon his head the <s>Gaṅgā</s>-bathed,

children.text: sacchidraṃ nṛśiraḥkapālamamalaṃ candraṃ ca dhatte samam /
children.translated_text: the flawed human skull, and the spotless moon.
The moon is even more pitiable, who, even when such an insult exists,
with his body pale from the bloom of moonlight-laughter, cherishes supreme delight. //
When full, with wave-arms, the ocean eagerly embraces the moon in the flush of its swelling,

children.text: kṣīṇaṃ dūrata eva muñcati pitā bhūtvā jalānāṃ nidhiḥ /
children.translated_text: when waning, he releases it from afar — though he is the father, the treasury of waters.

children.text: prakṣīṇasya tu yena tasya vasunā kṛtvā krameṇodayaṃ
children.translated_text: But by whose wealth, having gradually caused the rise of that waning one,

children.text: pūrṇatve ca davīyasi sthitamaho mitrāya tasmai namaḥ //
children.translated_text: and then standing far away at its fullness — ah! Salutations to that friend [the Sun]! //
When the lord of planets and earth, the god [Sun], stands far away, bound by darkness,
by whom indeed was his auspicious-wheeled, joy-bringing rising not longed for?

children.text: etenābhyuditena saṃprati punaḥ kaṣṭaṃ tathā ceṣṭitaṃ
children.translated_text: But now, having risen, alas, he has so acted
that 'this one is fierce-rayed' — people do not look at him face to face. //
Seeing whom with thousands of hands dispelling darkness,
the <s>piśācas</s> (demons) flee by the hundreds daily out of fear.
When the moon wanes and its rays are stolen by <s>Hari</s> (the Sun), it is wondrous —
one cloud-demon alone seizes that jewel of the sky. //
The sun is ever ready to rescue the entire world swallowed by darkness;

children.text: taṃ tu trātuṃ tamograstaṃ jagatyekopi na kṣamaḥ //
children.translated_text: but to rescue him when swallowed by darkness, not a single one in the world is able. //
At night, from the lotus — that treasury of virtues — the <s>kumuda</s> (night-lily) gained imperishable glory;

children.text: prāptā lakṣmīḥ sa mahimā rājño jaḍanidherdhruvam //
children.translated_text: that greatness was surely attained from the king, a treasury of dullness. //
The night never shines without the moon,
and the moon too, without the night, is one whose beauty is gone.
What is the reason that between these two, once every month,
there occurs a union of embrace, born of their thinness? //
Leaving the night lying on the bed of the sky, the moon
departs in the bright fortnight, while in the dark fortnight, the night [departs].
When the moon withdraws from the sleeping night upon the couch of the sky,
does their conjugal bond break by just so much? //
He who illuminates the directions, shattering the darkness,
who gives vision to the eyes, who is cherished for [his] abundant virtues —
whose beneficence to others causes no distress even in excess —
what wise person does not bow to that praiseworthy sun? //

children.text: vicārastathyo vā bhavatu vitatho vā kimaparaṃ
children.translated_text: Let the inquiry be true or false — what else [matters]?
Nevertheless, there is much talk and clamor among people about one of great splendor.
Even of the Sun — who has surpassed all measure, whose fame is renowned and whose darkness is destroyed —

children.text: ravestādṛktejo na bhavati hi kanyāṃ gata iti //
children.translated_text: such brilliance does not exist, [they say], once he has entered [the sign of] the maiden (<s>Kanyā</s>/Virgo). //
Surrounded by hosts of stars, the lord of herbs (<s>Oṣadhīpati</s>, the Moon),
with a body made of <s>amṛta</s> (nectar), endowed with beauty — even the moon,
upon reaching the orb of the sun, becomes rayless.
Who, dwelling in another's abode, does not come to insignificance? //
'I am lofty, I yield good fruit, I too am like this' — with just so much,

children.text: spardhāṃ manda madoddhataḥ svajanakenārkeṇa mā mā kṛthāḥ /
children.translated_text: O foolish one, puffed up with pride, do not, do not make rivalry with the Sun through your own people!

children.text: dūrādeva bhavādṛśosya mahasā dhvastāḥ samastāḥ svayaṃ
children.translated_text: From afar alone, by his brilliance, all like you are destroyed on their own.
He does not even desire the downfall [of anyone]; that treasury of splendor is a friend of the virtuous. //
'My comfortable position is equal to his' — thus with the king,
in sport with one's own father, the cause of [one's] birth —

children.text: mā rājanandana kṛthāḥ sa hi sarvaloka-
children.translated_text: O prince, do not make rivalry! For he is the destroyer of darkness for all the worlds,
one whose self is purified by the hand of <s>Giriśa</s> (<s>Śiva</s>). //
Abandoning the planets out of envy, knowing his own fitness for the dissimilar [realm of] fire and smoke,
the Sun creates his radiance, inclined toward the cessation of mockery.

children.text: daivaṃ vetti na yaḥ śikhī sa parato nāmāstu tatsaṃbhavāḥ
children.translated_text: The fire (<s>Śikhī</s>), who does not know fate — let that [merely] be its name; but born from that [Sun],
there would be lamps too, by whose power the world forgets the fierce-rayed one. //

children.text: pādmā ye madanuvratā dadhati te klāntiṃ tuṣārāhatā
children.translated_text: Those lotuses (<s>Pādmā</s>) who follow me suffer exhaustion, struck by frost;

children.text: yepyete divasā madekaśaraṇāḥ kārśyaṃ paraṃ yānti te /
children.translated_text: these days too, whose sole refuge I am, become extremely emaciated.
Thus departing to a far region, as if out of love for those who depend on him,
in winter the blessed lord of day — ah! — has gone! Let the world be served! //

children.text: nābhiṣeko na saṃskāraḥ siṃhasya kriyate vane /
children.translated_text: No <s>abhiṣeka</s> (consecration) is performed, no <s>saṃskāra</s> (investiture) is given to the lion in the forest.
For one whose nobility is won by valor alone, kingship over beasts comes of itself. //
'I am alone, I have no companion, I am thin, I lack retinue' —
such anxiety never arises, even in a dream, for the lord of beasts. //
Whose claws are thunderbolts, hard enough to split the frontal globes of maddened elephants —
the lion (<s>Kesarī</s>) comes to diminishment by the very name 'enemy of deer' (<s>mṛgāri</s>). //
The fierce claws of the lion, eager to split the frontal globes of elephants,
do not fall even upon bounding deer. //
Who is the worm? Who is to be blamed when this is the incongruity?

children.text: kākiṇyapi na siṃhasya mūlyaṃ koṭistu dantinaḥ //
children.translated_text: The lion's worth is not even a <s>kākiṇī</s> (small coin), while the elephant's is in the crores! //
Of him whose sport has shattered the frontal mounds of bold elephants —

children.text: kathaṃ kesariṇaḥ krāntaṃ suptasyāpi mṛgaiḥ padam //
children.translated_text: how can deer tread upon the domain of the lion, even when he sleeps? //
By the lion, whose paws are reddened with blood from splitting the frontal globes of maddened elephants —

children.text: hariṇā hariṇaḥ spardhāṃ varākaḥ kurute katham //
children.translated_text: how does the wretched deer presume to make rivalry with <s>Hari</s> (the lion)? //
The elephant trumpets in the forest, sluggish with the weight of <s>mada</s> (rut-fluid),
only so long as the lion has not arrived, with his tail curled over his head. //
Of one whose cheeks glow, breathing [heavily] from pride inflated by courage,
having plucked the mane of the lion — do men sit in comfort? //
The maddened elephant falls from a single slap of one paw in anger —
in a fight between <s>Hari</s> (the lion) and deer, how great is the extent of effort? //
As long as the claws of the lion are fastened upon the bones for an instant,
so long lasts the life of that forest-dwelling herd. //
Of him whose fierce valor's course is the shattering
of the cheek-regions of all roaring elephants,
how does the lion accept engagement
in a contest with endlessly resting deer? //
Even a lion cub pounces upon elephants whose cheek-surfaces are stained with rut-fluid.

children.text: prakṛtiriyaṃ sattvavatāṃ na khalu vayastejaso hetuḥ //
children.translated_text: This is the nature of the valiant — age is certainly not the cause of prowess. //
Dwelling alone in the forest, without royal insignia, unknowing of political treatises,
for the lord of beasts, exalted in spirit, the words 'king' come true. //
The lion displays his valor upon the trunk of the elephant, marked with dark rut-streaks,
but not upon the mongoose lodged in the mountain cave scratched by his claws. //
Of the lion whose tawny mane is smeared with the rut-fluid from splitting the frontal globes of maddened elephants,
who indeed dares to place a hand upon the mouth? //
When hundreds of unrestrained elephant calves,
foolishly frolic and wander about even in front [of him],
for the lion, whose mind is accustomed to splitting the frontal globes of maddened elephants,
merely closing his eyes is the proper [response]. //
Seeing the enemy of deer (<s>mṛgāri</s>, the lion) approaching like Death himself, with mane-clad shoulders rolling in rage,
right before them,
flocks of flesh-desiring vultures swooped down,
hovering upon the heads of the rut-blinded elephant herd-leaders. //
