That lion, who with fierce paws [like] saws of sharp claws
had torn open the excellent frontal globes of noble elephants,
and whose thirst was quenched by the fresh flood of blood —
alas! Shame! Today he competes with a blade of grass. //
His body reeks [of blood], his mind is inclined to slaying others,
his discernment of good and bad is declared as [mere] animal nature.
Thus nothing whatsoever is virtuous about the lord of beasts,
yet his splendor blazes, by which the world is wretched. //
Whether the lion is an enemy or the overlord of beasts —
I do not consider either of the two a cause for praise.
Of him whose playful blow of claw-tips [hard as] thunderbolts upon the head
effortlessly topples the moving mountain that is the elephant. //
In the cave of <s>Hari</s> (the lion), where the swaying radiance of claw-strokes has been embedded
in renowned herds of elephants,
a jackal, whose boldness was destroyed merely by that [lion's] distant glance, a wretch of vile essence,
has entered — alas! What a painful sight today! //
With teeth active in the delightful splitting of the frontal globes of maddened elephants,
with blows from the tips of his claw-thunderbolts resounding —
would the lion, that treasury of pride, in this world, sustain his bodily existence
with a blade of grass, even at the cost of his life? //
O lion, do not leap upon the cloud that thunders aloft in its station, bearing a bow for the world's sustenance,
with your mind rendered unruly by the arrogance of [defeating] elephant-rut!
From our mountain shattered by [<s>Indra</s>'s] thunderbolt, [the cloud] protects with showers of hailstones —
from the fall arising from the eagerness to leap, contemplate the destruction of your own body. //
Of the lion, whose ground is adorned with pearls
fallen from the lofty frontal globes of elephants pierced by his sharp claws,
does a herd of deer annul the enmity of <s>Hari</s> (the lion) in battle,
even when assembled together from all sides, all united in one purpose? //
The lion playfully shatters with fierce claws the elephants
whose cheek-slopes are adorned with rut-fluid imitating rocky mountains,
buzzing with dense clusters of bees, resonant with deep humming.

children.text: trijagati teja eva guru no vikṛtākṛtitā //
children.translated_text: In the three worlds, it is splendor alone that is weighty, not distorted appearance. //
O heroic lord, be not angry at the lord of beasts dwelling in mountain-range cave-homes,
living by his own splendor, of effortless and exalted valor.
From our [side], with minds troubled by passion,
whose sole sport and motive is drinking the marrow from elephant frontal globes — let what has been obtained by oneself be considered. //
Of the king named <s>Mīrashāh</s>, who desired to go to <s>Kaśmīra</s>,
the king <s>Shāhābuddīna</s> sent a letter thus: //
'Why, O young deer, so fearlessly, with frolicking gait,
do you desire to roam about? Desist! The forest is not empty.',
'Here stands the lion, with a mass of bristling mane, brilliant with the splashing streams
of blood from the slaughter by the lord of the elephant-host.' //
The lion, whose mane rolls about, reddened by the blood flowing
from the frontal platforms of elephants struck by [his] hard claws,
is ashamed of the battlefield, with the falling deer
whose trembling, terrified, exceedingly frightened cries [are heard] amidst the deep roaring. //
'Roam freely, O bulls, and eat the flesh of the net as you wish, fearless;
drink again, O buffaloes, the clear water at the edges of the lotus ponds;

children.text: vahata kariṇo bhūyaḥ śobhāṃ madena kapolayor-
children.translated_text: bear again, O elephants, the beauty of rut-fluid on your cheeks' —
the lion has departed far, unable to endure. //
'Having obtained arrogance [of power], seeing the cloud thundering in the sky, that

children.text: dūrāducchalitosi siṃha mahatāṃ tenaiva khinnaṃ manaḥ /
children.translated_text: you have leapt up from afar, O lion — by that very [act] the minds of the great are pained.'
'That you now face the mouth of the cave out of fear of the downpour —

children.text: taddṛṣṭvaiva vayaṃ hriyā kimaparaṃ pātālamūlaṃ gatāḥ //
children.translated_text: seeing just that, we have gone to the netherworld's depths in shame.' //
He whose sole delight was the unruly pastime of time [itself],
the splitting of the frontal platforms of many rut-blinded elephant hosts,
he who rivaled the dense, heavy rain-bearing clouds with his roar — that very lion
now, with body confined by the fall into a cage, endures such a condition! //
Though emaciated by hunger, though wasted by old age, though his life-breaths are feeble, though fallen into a wretched state,
though ruined in resolve and wisdom, though his very life-breaths are perishing,
his claw-tips are thunderbolts, swaying as they split the frontal globes of pride-swollen lord-elephants
Does the lion, foremost in greatness of pride, eat withered grass? //

children.text: nāsyocchrāyavatī tanurna daśanau no dīrghadīrghaḥ karaḥ
children.translated_text: His body is not towering tall, nor are his teeth, nor is his trunk long and long —
Truly, O elephant, this lion cub does not compete with your pomp /
But an irresistible seed of splendor was placed in his heart long ago by <s>Brahmā</s> (the Creator),

children.text: tādṛktvādṛśameva yena sutarāṃ bhojyaṃ paśuṃ manyate //
children.translated_text: by which he regards one such as you as merely prey to be easily devoured //
With the thick fat from the temples of intoxicated elephants, the lingering scent of musk,
the scattered pearl-fragments glistening on his mane, making him fearsome /
Inflicting the afflictions of widowhood, his splendor consuming the pride of heroes by the strength of his own arms,
the herds of <s>sāraṅgas</s> (deer) fleeing in terror — who has ever seen such an ever-intolerant lion? //

children.text: kaḥ kaḥ kutra na ghurghurāyitaghurīghoro ghuretsūkaraḥ
children.translated_text: What boar anywhere is not fearsome with its fierce, growling grunts?

children.text: kaḥ kaḥ kaṃ kamalākaraṃ vikamalaṃ kartuṃ karī nodyataḥ /
children.translated_text: What elephant anywhere does not rise up to strip the lotus-ponds of their lotuses? /
What wild buffaloes anywhere would not uproot which forests? And yet,
the five-faced one (<s>Siṃha</s>, the lion) dwells with his abode bound by the playful affection of the lioness //
He who from childhood itself has delighted in the lukewarm blood-essence
flowing from the split temple-regions of elephants maddened with rut, thrilling like one tasting <s>muktā-pulāka</s> (pearl-rice) /
How could his paw ever advance, even in the direst extremity,
toward seizing the life of a hare rolling about in a pit — that paw of <s>Hari</s> (the lion)! //
Even the herds of primal suns, resembling his claw-tips smeared with blood,
fled, having escaped into the <s>palāśa</s> (flame-of-the-forest) groves /

children.text: siṃhasya tasya jarato viṣamā daśā yad-
children.translated_text: Such is the dire condition of that aged lion, that
he cannot even sustain himself on the limbs of jackals, his enemies //
He who roared against the thundercloud, who chased the wind-borne

children.text: nambhodhīniva dhāvataḥ sarabhasaṃ hatvā raṇe vāraṇān /
children.translated_text: deputies of the <s>Vindhya</s> mountains like oceans, having slain elephants impetuously in battle /
Even upon a small-bodied monkey leaping from tree to tree

children.text: kruddhaḥ sopi bhavānaho bata gataḥ pañcāsya hāsyāṃ daśām //
children.translated_text: he too was enraged — alas, O five-faced one, he has now arrived at a pitiable state! //
Having led the troops of elephants, intoxicated with rut,
whose mountain-peak splendors were put to shame by his roars imitating thunder, skilled in scornful humiliation /
The lion, whose proven prowess is known to all the world, when the jackals of foul abode
torment him in concert from all ten directions — does he even bestir himself against them? //
O young elephant, abandon your waywardness,
walk the path of discipline with bowed face /
That which is fragile before the claw-tips of the lord of beasts —
the heavy goad upon you cannot endure as much //
Play your games, feast upon lotuses,
plunge into the waters of mountain-slope cascades /
O <s>Mātaṅga</s> (elephant), with limbs caressed by the trunk of a lovingly devoted she-elephant,
abandon your desire for battle with the king of beasts //
By this unruly elephant, intoxicated and heedless,
all this was thrown into confusion /
How then, by a mere boy of a <s>mahout</s>,

children.text: mandaḥ kathaṃ gamita eṣa vaśaṃ prasahya //
children.translated_text: was this sluggish one brought forcibly under control by placing a foot upon his head? //
With his trunk worshipped by heaps of pollen falling from the flowers
of the trees on the slopes of the <s>Vindhya</s> mountains, attended by elephant herds /
That very lord of elephants who was such — how has he now become
an executor of men's commands? Or is it that Time is the master here? //
O bull among elephants, with your body tormented by the fierce heat
of the fire of separation blazing within — abandon your grief! /
Who is able to erase the letters
inscribed upon the forehead by <s>Dhātā</s> (the Creator) with his own hand? //

children.text: bho bhoḥ karīndra divasāni kiyanti tāvad-
children.translated_text: Ho, ho, O lord of elephants, for however many days,
pass the time somehow or other in this desert! /
With the waters of the <s>Revā</s> (Narmadā) river, applied by your own she-elephant's trunk,
you shall again find relief when the hot season comes //
In this inert world, what elephant of great size
would not be a vessel of misfortune? /
Even that one who uprooted the fishing line that came [to trap him] —
it is the elephant alone [who suffers]; what then is there beyond this? //
He does not take his mouthful in the water fragrant with fresh lotus-pollen,
he finds no delight in mud or in half-broken lotus-fiber pieces /
He does not endure even another she-elephant who is affectionate and full of love,
the lord of elephants, remembering his beloved lost from the herd //
He does not take the tips of creepers, nor the water cool as a crescent moon;
he avoids the lovely lotus-beds with their attendant hovering bees /
The elephant, now love-bereaved, holding his trunk in the shape of a burden,
heaving sighs, does not rest even for a moment at the edge of the forest //
He who once split rivers like [barriers] before him, uprooted trees like tender shoots,
and conquered rival elephants maddened with rut with his trunk, feet, and tusks /
Having reached ignoble old age, which generates the contempt of the young,

children.text: sa evāyaṃ nāgaḥ sahati kalabhebhyaḥ paribhavam //
children.translated_text: that very same elephant now endures insults from young calves //
Better is this wound from the goad, unnoticed as it falls
upon your head, O leader of the elephant-herd, out of a desire for discipline /
Than the final blow of the adamantine claw-tips,
sharp and forcibly risen, of the forest-dwelling lion //
Abandoning your own free-roaming she-elephant at the edge of the mountain range in the forest,
your mind has fallen upon city-folk devoid of true affection /
This fruit — consisting of the toil of binding with stout ropes, confinement, and punishment —

children.text: he mattadvipu karmaṇaḥ pariṇataṃ rāgānurūpaṃ phalam //
children.translated_text: O intoxicated elephant, has ripened as a consequence fitting your passion! //

children.text: kvākāro girisannibhaḥ kva ca gatirvegena līlā ca sā
children.translated_text: Where is that mountain-like form? Where is that gait of speed and that playful grace?

children.text: helākuḍmalitekṣaṇāḥ kva nu dṛśastadvā kva te bṛṃhitam /
children.translated_text: Where are those glances with half-closed eyes of disdain? Where is that trumpeting? /

children.text: vaprāghātarasaḥ kva te kva ca karaḥ kaṣṭaṃ yadevaṃvidhaṃ
children.translated_text: Where is your delight in striking ramparts? Where is that trunk? Alas, that in this very state
a boy, having mounted upon you, directs you, helpless, by command with his feet! //
The earth trembled from the stamping of his feet; the birds grew sluggish with fear;
the ponds were marked with mud; the trees were shattered by the rubbing of his cheeks /
Having found this forest free of tigers by fate, the young elephants

children.text: tattannāma kṛtaṃ viśṛṅkhalatayā vaktuṃ na yatpāryate //
children.translated_text: performed such feats of unbridled freedom that cannot be described //
Even while eating sugar-cane, and also meat-rice dishes rich with ghee,
even while being covered with various blankets and wearing garlands of stars /
Even while bearing a garland of fly-whisks upon his ears, the tusked one still
remains ever sorrowful, remembering the dense <s>sallakī</s>-tree forests of the <s>Vindhya</s> hills //
He who was raised in infancy on handfuls of the tips of wild rice,
who drank the remnant-milk of oblations from a lotus-leaf cup /
Seeing that elephant now, slow-moving with the swaying garland of rut, with streaming temples,

children.text: sotkaṇṭhaṃ sabhayaṃ ca paśyati muhurdūre sthitastāpasaḥ //
children.translated_text: the ascetic standing at a distance gazes again and again, with longing and with fear //

children.text: dante nyasya karaṃ pralambitaśirāḥ saṃmīlya netradvayaṃ
children.translated_text: Resting his trunk upon his tusk, hanging his head, closing both eyes —

children.text: kiṃ tvaṃ vāraṇa tapyase gaṇikayā ko nāma no vañcitaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Why, O elephant, do you grieve? By a courtesan — who indeed has not been deceived? /

children.text: grāsaṃ śāntamanā gṛhāṇa satataṃ śokodhunā tyajyatāṃ
children.translated_text: Take your morsel with a calm mind; abandon your sorrow now.',
'Those who are intoxicated, undiscriminating, and fickle-minded — they encounter calamity' //
She whose livelihood was made from the morsels of food left over by her lord,
who drank the water remaining after he had muddied it by plunging his trunk /

children.text: prāṇānpūrvataraṃ vihāya tadidaṃ prāptaṃ kariṇyā phalaṃ
children.translated_text: Having given up her life-breaths before [him], this is the fruit obtained by the she-elephant:

children.text: yadbandhārpaṇakātarasya kariṇaḥ kliṣṭaṃ na dṛṣṭaṃ mukham //
children.translated_text: that she did not behold the anguished face of her elephant-lord, distressed at being offered in captivity //

children.text: ghāsagrāsaṃ gṛhāṇa tyaja gajakalabha premabandhaṃ kariṇyāḥ
children.translated_text: 'Take your mouthful of grass, abandon, O young elephant, the bond of love for the she-elephant;
now apply the mud-ointment, the remedy for the wounds of the knots of your fetters /
Far from you now are these <s>Vindhya</s> foot-hills, dusky with the flower-pollen
of the trees upon the banks of the <s>Revā</s>, lovely with the wandering charm of forest-women' //
The wagging of the tail, the falling down of the feet below,
lying on the ground, and showing the face and belly /
A dog does this for the one who gives a morsel; but the noble elephant
gazes with dignity and eats only after hundreds of entreaties //
That the <s>Vindhya</s> is peaked, and that within it is the <s>pippala</s> (fig tree) dear to the <s>pīlu</s>,
and that the she-elephant, longing, rushes impetuously — /

children.text: tatkiṃ bhadratayā smaratyapi karī daivaṃ hi sarvaṃkaṣaṃ
children.translated_text: Does the elephant remember all that with equanimity? For fate is all-consuming.

children.text: tanmṛtyorapi duḥsahaṃ tu yadayaṃ mando dhuri sthāpitaḥ //
children.translated_text: And what is most unbearable even for death itself — this dull one has been yoked to the cart! //
He who grew up amid the <s>Vindhya</s>, amidst the breezes wafting the soft
jasmine-buds scattered by the playful gusts from the waves of the <s>Narmadā</s> river /
That very elephant, now bereft of freedom by the decree of fate, trumpeting piteously,
helpless in the grip of wet ropes and nooses — alas, what can he do! //
O <s>gandha-kuñjara</s> (elephant of the fragrant ichor), O foremost of great mountain-elephants,
even now, do not reminisce with playfully half-closed eyes! /
Abandon your pride now; accept the present [condition],
and the crooked commandment of <s>Vidhi</s> (fate) upon you — and the goad //

children.text: svacchasvādujalā vihāya sarito hartuṃ tṛṣaṃ duḥsahāṃ
children.translated_text: 'Having forsaken the rivers of clear, sweet water to quell your unbearable thirst,

children.text: mā matta dviradākṣi nikṣipa śaratkṛṣṭe taḍāgāmbuni /
children.translated_text: O intoxicated elephant, do not cast your eye upon the shrunken autumn pond-water /

children.text: pītesminsakalepi gacchati na te śāntiṃ pipāsā jale
children.translated_text: Even if all this water is drunk, your thirst will not find peace in it;
and for this village with its single water-source, there would surely be danger to its livelihood' //
Blessed are the deer in the forest, feeding on <s>dūrvā</s>-grass shoots and grass,
for they do not behold the faces of those whose minds are intoxicated with wealth! //
Lifeless, devoid of breath, with the inner arrow's wound unhealed,
the doe lies unbound, motionless, near the decoy-deer //
The directions are strung with ropes, the water with poison,
the earth with snares, the forest-ends set ablaze with fire /
The hunters follow the tracks, arrows in hand —
to what region can the leader of the deer-herd resort? //
Go swiftly from here, O deer, or you will be separated from your life-breaths!
Why do you stand with neck turned, looking back again and again? /
These glances of yours do not produce even the slightest tenderness
in these hunters of hard hearts //
Chasing the mirage over the scorched flatlands,

children.text: tṛṣārtaḥ sāraṅgo viramati na khinnepi manasi /
children.translated_text: the thirsty <s>sāraṅga</s> (deer) does not cease even when his mind is wearied /
Not knowing the truth, he does not seek a pond elsewhere —

children.text: mabhūmau pratyāśā na ca phalati vighnaṃ ca kurute //
children.translated_text: hope in a barren place does not bear fruit and only creates obstacles //
O <s>sāraṅga</s> (deer), eat the grass, sustain your life-breaths with water — or else,

children.text: yadvā syāḥ pavanāśanastadapi te sāviṣkṛti prāṇitam /
children.translated_text: even if you were to subsist on air alone, that too would be a manifest way of living /
So that this gaze of yours, beautiful as the expanse of blooming blue lotuses,
may not be exhausted upon the face of a fool with eyes haughty with the pride of wealth //
Where there is a fall from the slightest stumble, where rising is difficult,
where entry is hard through the thicket of bamboo-creeper canopies at the gate /
O <s>sāraṅga</s> (deer), having abandoned the delightful forest grounds, striving for special gain,
why have your hooves been worn away in vain, addicted to dwelling in the mountain fortress? //
These are not the forest-lands of <s>Malaya</s> with their crystal-clear flowing cascades,
in which the thirst of embodied beings is quenched by merely beholding them /
This is <s>Bharu</s> (a desert), haunted by harsh crows, with expanding bewilderments —

children.text: tā etā mṛgatṛṣṇikā hariṇa he nedaṃ payo gamyatām //
children.translated_text: those are mirages, O deer — this is not water; turn back! //

children.text: tyaktaṃ janmavanaṃ tṛṇāṅkuravatī māteva muktā sthalī
children.translated_text: The birth-forest was abandoned; the earth with its grass-shoots, like a mother, was forsaken;
the trees, like kinsmen providing grounds for trust, were not regarded /
That doe, distressed by the grief of separation from her young, was not heeded —

children.text: mārgantaḥ padavīṃ tathāpyakaruṇā vyādhā na muñcantyamī //
children.translated_text: yet even so, these merciless hunters do not release [the deer] from the path //
Having cut the snare, cast off the decoy-trap, broken through the hunting-net by force,
and escaping far from the forest bristling with garlands of blazing fire-tips /
Even leaping swiftly beyond the arrow-range of the hunters, the running deer

children.text: kūpāntaḥ patitaḥ karoti vidhure kiṃ vā vidhau pauruṣam //
children.translated_text: fell into a well — what valor avails against fate in its cruelty? //

children.text: svairī bhrāmyasi nātha kāmyasi paradvārāṇi nottāmyasi
children.translated_text: You wander at will, you frequent others' doors, you do not grow weary,
you do not see the faces of mistresses twisted with causeless anger /

children.text: muñcasyekamapi kṣaṇaṃ prakaṭitapremāṃ ca na preyasīṃ
children.translated_text: You do not abandon even for a moment your beloved who has displayed her love openly —
O <s>sāraṅga</s> (deer), who taught you this exceedingly beautiful vow? //
The fresh cluster of rice-shoots, dripping with milk from their breaking,
which the freely roaming deer happened upon by chance /
With inner agony proclaimed by the scorched tender grass of his sighs,
he meditates upon her alone day after day, like a sage, and wastes away in the forest //

children.text: sāraṅgo na latāgṛheṣu ramate no paṃsule bhūtale
children.translated_text: The <s>sāraṅga</s> (deer) does not delight in the bower-houses, nor on the dusty ground
not in the lovely cool green shade at the edges of forests, /
constantly meditating day after day upon that long-eyed beloved,
he stands with mind withdrawn in the caves of great mountains, wearing the garb of an ascetic. //
He scratches the bodies of deer with his horn to gain the trust of the indifferent ones,
moving about slowly at his own will, he avoids from fear the abode of the herd-leader. /
Seen, he stands unnoticed — struck suddenly by the sidelong glances of doe,
the <s>sāraṅga</s> (deer) dwells in misery, having entered another herd by the force of cruel fate. //
Having taken all the flesh from my limbs except the breasts —

children.text: māṃ muñca vāgurika yāhi kuru prasādam /
children.translated_text: release me, O fowler! Go, show mercy! /
Still ignorant of swallowing a morsel of grass,
my young one is intent on watching for my path [home]. //
Before lies the <s>Revā</s> (Narmadā), beyond it a mountain with an exceedingly difficult peak to climb,
a lake to the right, on the left the conflagration of a forest fire. /
Behind, a wretched <s>Śabara</s> (hunter) with bow in hand runs swiftly —

children.text: na yātuṃ na sthātuṃ hariṇāśiśureṣa prabhavati //
children.translated_text: this fawn can neither go nor stand still. //

children.text: kva krīḍati kva carati kva karoti vṛttiṃ
children.translated_text: Where does it play? Where does it wander? Where does it seek its food?

children.text: vāri kva nāma pibati svapiti kva nāma /
children.translated_text: Where indeed does it drink water? Where indeed does it sleep? /
Thus, the hunter pursues to kill the innocent, inoffensive deer,
wielding his bow. //
The moon is the nectar-rayed one, <s>Yama</s> is the son of the sun, <s>Bṛhaspati</s> is the lord of the twice-born,
attained through merits — 'he has come to me for refuge' — thus [the deer felt] satisfaction. /
O innocent fawn, worship [them], do not abandon [hope] — [but] wicked is this
one who, having swallowed a fish, has immediately taken on the form of a ram! //
O young camel, if ever by a stroke of fate you should wander
and obtain honey from a swarm of bees, /
desist, desist from them! There are grasses in the wilderness —
those [bees], noisy at first, will only dry you up later! //
Leaving behind the forest ground adorned with lakes blooming with open <s>kumuda</s> (night-lotuses) and full-blown lotuses,
green as emerald gems with tender grass, /
the young camel, wandering among the trees of the desert, remembers [it] —

children.text: paricayaratiḥ sā durvārā na sā guṇavairitā //
children.translated_text: that is the irresistible love of familiarity, not hostility to virtues. //
O beloved of the young camel, that honey obtained once with difficulty
from the forest — in its absence, why do you cry out eagerly? /
Be content with the familiar leaves of the <s>pīlu</s> tree in the desert region —
in this entire world, who attains uninterrupted happiness? //
O beloved of the young camel, that <s>pīlu</s> tree which you, greedy for honey,
abandoned without a caring glance, stripped of its wealth and shade — /
that very tree now, with trembling shoots and fresh new sprouts,
is happily enjoyed by other herds of young she-camels. //
O young camel, why do you waste your little body with long sighs?

children.text: virama śaṭhe he kasyātyantaṃ sakhe sukhamāgatam /
children.translated_text: Desist, O rogue! — O friend, to whom has perpetual happiness ever come? /
Walk about at ease, eat the tender shoots, abandon the longing for honey from the <s>pīlu</s> tree —
you shall again become a vessel of good fortune. //
O young camel, you eagerly wish to cry out — ah, a fever to the ears!
Or perhaps your long, upright neck is your refuge. /
The voice, wearied by the effort of passing through the broad cavity of the throat, will issue forth from the mouth —

children.text: diyati samaye ko jānīte bhaviṣyati kasya kim //
children.translated_text: in time, who knows what will happen to whom? //
Thus, content, wandering at ease in the forest among <s>sañjala</s>, <s>vṛṇa</s>, <s>śamī</s>, <s>pīlu</s>, and <s>badara</s> trees,
the young camel-calf was free from sorrow. /
But foolish fate made his heart inclined to the taste of honey,

children.text: yathā nānyadbhuṅkte na pibati na śete na ramate //
children.translated_text: so that he neither eats anything else, nor drinks, nor sleeps, nor takes delight. //
He for whom even a mouthful of fresh <s>pīlu</s> leaves and <s>badara</s> fruit was sufficient for contentment,
whose path is not followed even by his own herd-mates on the long road — /

children.text: soyaṃ saṃprati yāti bālakarabhaḥ kṣīṇodyamaḥ kṣāmatāṃ
children.translated_text: that same young camel now goes, his efforts exhausted, toward emaciation;
I think, surely, struck by fate, he has tasted the honey of the bee! //

children.text: pīlūnāṃ hi phalaṃ kaṣāyarahitaṃ romanthayitvā marau
children.translated_text: Having chewed in the desert the astringency-free fruit of <s>pīlu</s> trees,
and that lovely branch-tip which was placed in the she-camel's mouth with love — /

children.text: tatsmṛtvā karabhena khedavidhuraṃ dīrghaṃ tathā kūjitaṃ
children.translated_text: remembering that, the young camel bellowed long and piteously,
and that very [cry] suddenly became like the departure-trumpet of his life-breaths. //
One who desires what is tender despises the camel;
the camel, fond of thorns, [despises] that one. /
When the two, each enjoying what they prefer, are equal [in satisfaction],
neutrality [is proper], not ridicule of either side. //

children.text: eka eva khago mānī vane vasati cātakaḥ /
children.translated_text: One single proud bird dwells in the forest — the <s>cātaka</s> (rain-bird). /

children.text: pipāsito vā mriyate yācate vā puraṃdaram //
children.translated_text: It either dies of thirst or begs only of <s>Purandara</s> (Indra). //

children.text: ayi cakitamugdhacātaka marubhuvi dhāvasi mudhā kimudgrīvam /
children.translated_text: O startled, innocent <s>cātaka</s>, why do you run vainly through the desert with neck upraised? /
In summer, enveloped by forest fire, this is [only] a <s>tāmāla</s> tree's [smoke], not lightning! //
Even when thirsty, the peacock
waits for its beloved [peahen] to drink, regarding [her] as equal to [its own] life. /
Surely, with eyes bound by love for the beloved,
it sees little water in the streams. //
Let this chick of the <s>cātaka</s>, given to the vice of excessive pride,
bestow its affection upon the shaking of its own head. /
For it does not desire these [waters] — in all the extended directions,

children.text: tāḥ svacchaśītamadhurāḥ kva nu nāma nāpaḥ //
children.translated_text: where indeed are there no waters that are clear, cool, and sweet? //
Beautiful with the splendor of its plumage, adorning the forests with its melodious cries,
this is the charm of the crested peacock. /
Yet as an ill-omened [creature], even though the sky is trodden by crows and the like,
it has never become equal to a sparrow in flight! //
Leaving behind the limpid water-bodies, purer in taste than nectar,
reddened by the pollen of blue lotuses, /
the <s>cātaka</s> drinks only the drops from rain-clouds —
I think it is the pride of [maintaining] one's dignity, not fear of bending [its head]. //
Your vow of drinking only celestial water — whom would it not delude?

children.text: doṣopi saṃvṛtimatāṃ bhajate guṇatvam bhūmisthamambu yadi cātaka pātumiccheḥ
children.translated_text: Even a fault assumes the nature of a virtue in those who possess self-restraint. If, O <s>cātaka</s>, you wished to drink water resting on the ground,
you would expose the wound on your throat and your unworthiness. //
Your vow of drinking only celestial water — whom would it not delude?
Even a fault assumes the nature of a virtue in those who possess self-restraint. //
Are there not water-bodies encircled by rows of swans,
adorned with fresh lotuses as crest-ornaments? /
Some powerful fate indeed holds the <s>cātaka</s>,
that it longs for the rain-shower of <s>Indra</s>'s clouds. //

children.text: kiṃ dūreṇa payodharā upari kiṃ nānye raṭantaḥ śrutā
children.translated_text: Why [look] far? Are there not clouds above? Have not other crying ones been heard?

children.text: nindyāḥ pāpatayā svakukṣiṣu gatāḥ kiṃ nāma pakṣāḥ kṣayam /
children.translated_text: Are the wings, gone to ruin within their own bodies, to be blamed as sinful? /

children.text: ramyaṃ vā gagane na kiṃ viharaṇaṃ kiṃ tūgrakākāvalī-
children.translated_text: Is not soaring in the sky delightful? Is it then from fear of the disgrace
of being taken turn by turn among the fierce crow-flocks that peacocks remain on the ground? //
Not by its dance that is a cascade of nectar for the eyes,
nor by its cry that is an elixir for the ears, /
nor even by its plumage that rivals the splendor of the rainbow of the gods —
is one satisfied with the peacock, without [tasting] its flesh. //
O dear <s>cātaka</s>, how much immeasurable sin have you committed?

children.text: navajaladādapi cañcupuṭe yattava na patati vāri //
children.translated_text: That from a fresh rain-cloud also, not a drop of water falls into your beak! //
Devoid of bestowing drops of water, displaying a whitish appearance — /

children.text: cātaka raṭasi vṛthā kiṃ jaladaḥ śārada eṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: O <s>cātaka</s>, why do you cry out in vain? This is an autumn cloud! //

children.text: santi kūpāḥ sphuradrūpāḥ paritaḥ saritaḥ śubhāḥ /
children.translated_text: There are wells of resplendent form, auspicious rivers all around; /
yet for the <s>cātaka</s>, the sole giver of fruit is the rising of rain-clouds. //
You utter sweet flatteries in the guise of <s>kekā</s> (cries),
and dance with your trembling plumage to delight [the cloud]. /
O <s>cātaka</s>, you strive thus before the cloud,

children.text: binduṃ jalasya labhase na ca lajjase ca //
children.translated_text: yet you obtain not a single drop of water — and still you feel no shame! //
O peacock, having been made the vehicle of the son of the Lord [<s>Kārttikeya</s>],
that very plumage of yours has withered. /
Have you not worshipped that Supreme Being [<s>Viṣṇu</s>]
who would quench your thirst with rain-showers from dark clouds? //
The <s>haṃsa</s>'s (swan's) identity as a swan is determined by
its dwelling with exceeding love in [Lake] <s>Mānasa</s>, its accustomed abode, not by [dwelling in] a mere puddle. //
Bees, dusky with pollen, drink honey from lotuses; /
swans eat moss — alas, how unjust is fate! //
If ever, by a turn of fate, the world were to become lotus-less,
would the <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), like a rooster, scatter heaps of rubbish? //
Where the garrulous <s>ṭiṭṭibha</s> (lapwing) bird chatters harshly nearby, /

children.text: apasaraṇameva śaraṇaṃ maunaṃ vā tatra haṃsasya //
children.translated_text: the only refuge for the <s>haṃsa</s> (swan) there is withdrawal, or silence. //
Although there may be water adorned with lotuses everywhere, /

children.text: ramate na marālasya mānasaṃ mānasaṃ vinā //
children.translated_text: the mind of the <s>marāla</s> (swan) does not delight without [Lake] <s>Mānasa</s>. //

children.text: kṣudhitopi padmakhaṇḍe jahāti rajasāvṛtaṃ hi kiṃjalkam /
children.translated_text: Even when hungry, the <s>haṃsa</s> (swan) abandons the pollen-covered filaments in a lotus patch; /

children.text: guṇini kṛtapakṣapāto bisaṃ tu bahu manyate haṃsaḥ //
children.translated_text: partial to virtue, it holds the <s>bisa</s> (lotus stalk) in high regard. //
Why do you dart your gaze eagerly,
O one cherished by the dwelling of an unstained mind? /
Descend into the pool, O <s>kalahaṃsī</s> (lovely goose),
you shall return again to the lotus-abode. //
Leaving behind the lovely <s>Himācala</s> (Himalayan) river, whose waters are filled with charming pollen of lotuses,
with beautiful songs of bee-maidens captivating the mind, /
O <s>haṃsa</s> (swan),

children.text: he he hatāśa vada kāṃ diśamutsukosi //
children.translated_text: alas, tell me — to what direction do you eagerly fly, O hopeless one? //
O <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), you who are capable of separating milk mixed with water —

children.text: śaktasya saṃprati matiḥ kva nu tedya yātā /
children.translated_text: where has your discernment gone today? /
For you wish to pick up in a pond the fallen reflection of the moon,
thinking it a lotus-stalk shoot! //
The holy, world-purifying, beautiful waters
of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s>, resting on the head of the moon-crested <s>Śiva</s>, /
having wandered long, obtained by fate —
do you wish to abandon them here? You are no <s>haṃsa</s> (swan)! //
Having stayed long in the sky with its motionless stars,
seeing a lotus-pond muddied by contact with elephants, /
the <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), with anger-swollen gurgling cry,

children.text: haṃsena sāśru parivṛtya gataṃ na līnam //
children.translated_text: turned away weeping, and did not alight. //
That lovely piece of lotus-stalk, white as snow and conch,
which was offered to the mouth of its companion — /
that same bird, O ill-fated one, by your doing,
now develops a fondness for bits of moss and stalks! //
Why do you caw harshly aloud, O crow, rivaling me?
O wretched bird, with the inside of your mouth stained red from excrement! /
I, whose wide white wing-strokes agitate the waters,
sporting among lotus-groves — I am a <s>sārasa</s> (crane), not a crow! //
A <s>haṃsa</s> (royal swan), a sky-traveler, entered at day's end
a grove of <s>kāraṇḍaka</s> (water-birds), crows, herons, and <s>bhāsa</s> (vultures) to rest from weariness. /
They mock him as mute and pluck his feathers —
taking refuge among the low is indeed the ground of humiliation for the great. //

children.text: kva kaṭhinamaho pīloḥ pattraṃ mṛduḥ kva bisāṅkuraḥ
children.translated_text: How harsh is the leaf of the <s>pīlu</s> — how tender the lotus-stalk!

children.text: kva kaṭu lavaṇaṃ kaupaṃ cāmbhaḥ kva tāmarasāsavaḥ /
children.translated_text: How bitter and salty the brackish water — how [sweet] the nectar of lotuses! /

children.text: kva kusumarajo hṛdyaṃ rūkṣāḥ kva coṣarapāṃsavaḥ
children.translated_text: How pleasant the pollen of flowers — how coarse the desert sands!

children.text: kva maruviṣayo dhvāṅkṣakṣetraṃ kva haṃsa bhavādṛśāḥ //
children.translated_text: What comparison between the desert, the realm of crows, and swans like you, O <s>haṃsa</s>? //
O royal <s>haṃsa</s>, why have you come here?

children.text: yosau bakaḥ sa iha haṃsa iti pratītaḥ /
children.translated_text: That crane there is reputed as a swan in this place. /
So depart quickly at dawn,
before the deluded people say, 'This is a crane!' //
O swans of the pond, do not make your hearts anxious —

children.text: karudhvaṃ mā ceto viyati bahato vīkṣya vihagān /
children.translated_text: a sign of the contraction of your own dwelling — upon seeing birds [flying] high in the sky! /
These are <s>sāraṅga</s> (cranes), upholders of the world-honored vow [of drinking only rain] —
for those who are desireless, even the oceans are [trivial] as grass. //
In a tree growing on the bank, with body hidden among the leaves,
pass this difficult rainy season with its falling torrents of rain. /
When it has passed, in the lake with lotuses fully blossoming,

children.text: sa eva tvaṃ haṃsaḥ punarapi vilāsāsta iha te //
children.translated_text: you shall be that same <s>haṃsa</s> (swan) again — here shall your pleasures resume. //
That depth [of the lake] is gone, the water too is covered with hundreds of nets;
O friend <s>haṃsa</s>, rise up first from this scorched lake! /
Lest — with body muddied by the mire-water, lamenting piteously —
the garrulous crow should place its feet upon your head! //

children.text: spṛśati na bisaṃ cañcvā bhūyastayā saha khaṇḍitaṃ
children.translated_text: It does not touch lotus-stalks with its beak, nor break and eat them as before with her [its mate];

children.text: pibati na jalaṃ yāti svaptuṃ na śevalajālakam /
children.translated_text: it does not drink water, nor go to sleep upon the bed of moss; /
the <s>sārasa</s> (crane) does not sport in the play of breaking lotus buds;
it calls out piteously, seized by grief, distressed by separation from its beloved. //
Repeatedly at night in the lake, biting the reflections of stars, being deceived,
the <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), searching for <s>kumuda</s> (night-lotus) stalks, proves inexpert in the dark. /
Then, suspicious of stars [even in daylight], it does not bite the white lotus by day either —
one deceived by trickery suspects danger even in the genuine. //
The waters [shine] like pearls, the lotus-stalk joints glitter with milky sap,
the nectar of lotuses is abundant, the sandy bank is fit for playful sport /
There are indeed, in every region, slightly uneven, O <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), mud-marked,
boldly-speaking-crane-infested, aging lakes — what is this attachment to dwelling [here]? //
May it again be filled with waters surging with waves of darting small fish,
may we again see that lake with lotuses being distributed about! —
with heart bound by a hundred threads of such hopes, day and night, with wretched mind,
the aged <s>sārasa</s> (crane) wastes away on the bank of the sun-dried lake. //
He who, radiant with the pollen-dust fallen from swaying lotuses as his body-paint,
hearing the melodious humming of the bees, was seized by the festival of joy —
unable even to grasp a morsel of lotus-stalk offered from his beloved's beak,

children.text: soyaṃ saṃprati haṃsako marugataḥ kaṣṭaṃ tṛṇaṃ vāñchati //
children.translated_text: that very <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), now gone to the desert, alas, craves mere grass! //
Remembering whom, they suddenly left <s>Mānasa</s> lake, desiring something special —
seeing that very <s>kamalinī</s> (lotus-pond) now occupied by cranes, with eager hearts,
those who, bereft of pride and lightened, alight there again —

children.text: haṃsāste na bhavanti haṃsadhavalāḥ prāyo bakā eva te //
children.translated_text: those <s>haṃsas</s> (swans) are not [true] swans, white as swans; they are mostly just cranes! //
Where cranes cling and cry harshly with long-sighing necks,
where these <s>madgus</s> (cormorants) leap about, their bodies rubbing against the shoulder-banks, disturbing the water,
which is constantly attended day and night by cranes of inherently impure nature —

children.text: sā haṃsena manasvinā kamalinī yuktaṃ yadi tyajyate //
children.translated_text: it is fitting indeed that a self-respecting <s>haṃsa</s> (swan) abandons such a <s>kamalinī</s> (lotus-pond)! //

children.text: rūpaṃ hāri manoharā sahacarī pānāya pādmaṃ madhu
children.translated_text: Charming form, a captivating companion, lotus-honey for drinking,

children.text: krīḍā cāpsu saroruheṣu vasatisteṣāṃ rajo maṇḍanam /
children.translated_text: play in the waters, dwelling on lotuses, their pollen as ornament,
a livelihood approved by the wise through lotus-stalks, friends the <s>ṣaṭpadas</s> (bees) with sweet voices —
the <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), free from the degradation of servile attendance and disrespect, lives happily. //
Even fish know the discrimination of milk from water;
the famous glory of <s>rājahaṃsas</s> (royal swans) is obtained through [accumulated] merit. //
Those who, even with wings torn by the fall of angry owl-talons, do not abandon their home —
those certain birds, whose bodies are nourished on dung, are one kind; //
but those reared on even a morsel of lotus-stalk from the celestial river,

children.text: gaṅgānīramapi tyajanti kaluṣaṃ te rājahaṃsāḥ kutaḥ //
children.translated_text: those <s>rājahaṃsas</s> (royal swans) — how could they abandon even the turbid waters of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>? //
Why do you utter such exceedingly soft words,
O male <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo), in this terrible [place] resounding with the heavy din of dull stones and jackals? //

children.text: kākaiḥ saha vivṛddhasya kokilasya kalā giraḥ /
children.translated_text: The melodious words of the <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo), though raised among crows —
how can harshness [come to] one whose nature is auspicious, even in the company of the wicked? //
O sweet-throated one, this melodious sound of yours, a feast for the ears,
the ambassador of the treaty of love's battle — who hears it
in these forest regions resounding with the harsh cries
from within the hollows of great trees burnt by forest fire? //

children.text: mūkīmūya tameva kokila madhuṃ bandhuṃ pratīkṣasva he
children.translated_text: Hush now and be silent, O <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo), wait for that friend, the spring,
with its breeze favorable to the fragrance of playfully blossoming <s>mālatī</s> jasmine —
where these songs of yours attain fruitfulness; but these blazing
summer days, filled with rising dust, are only producers of torment! //
Brother, enough of the cuckoo's cooing! Since virtues are not valued here,
remain silent, hidden somewhere in a hollow covered by heaps of withered leaves.
The time of winter is [here], with the garden trees crowded with harshly cawing flocks of crows —

children.text: kāloyaṃ śiśirasya saṃprati sakhe nāyaṃ vasantotsavaḥ //
children.translated_text: this, O friend, is not the festival of spring! //
Somewhere the chirping of crickets, somewhere the unmatched clamor of <s>kākola</s> birds,
somewhere the cry of herons, somewhere too the chattering of monkeys,
somewhere the dreadful howl of jackals — oh, the arrangement of fate!
How can the young <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo), frightened, sing its high-pitched song? //
The <s>bhṛṅga</s> (bee) attends upon the <s>ketakī</s> (screwpine) flower even when pricked by it;
what harm can faults do to one whose mind is captivated by virtues? //

children.text: kṛtvāpi koṣapānaṃ bhramarayuvā purata eva kamalinyāḥ /
children.translated_text: The young bee, even after drinking the nectar right before the lotus-pond,

children.text: abhilaṣati bakulakalikāṃ madhulihi maline kutaḥ satyam //
children.translated_text: desires the bud of the <s>bakula</s> tree — O honey-lover, faithless one, whence is there constancy? //
Having seen <s>Madana</s> (love) fruitless and the impermanence of the <s>bandhujīva</s> flowers,
approaching the teacher, the bee has now become devoted to <s>japā</s> (hibiscus/prayer). //
O <s>bhramara</s> (bee), having roamed to the ends of the quarters,
have you anywhere found, seen, or heard of —
tell truly, setting aside partiality —
a flower that rivals the <s>jātī</s> (jasmine) blossom? //
The lotus is his dwelling, pollen his body-ornament,
honey his drink, the sweet murmurings his beloved's prattle,
a soft bed of stamens his pillow —
what regal pleasure does the bee not [enjoy] upon the water? //
Falling, rising again, standing still, doing nothing,
buzzing pitifully, going and coming —
seeing the <s>kamalinī</s> (lotus-pond) now soiled and struck by frost,
there is nothing the [bee] has not done [in its grief]. //
The <s>kamalinī</s> (lotus-pond), soiled without its beloved, cannot endure
being attended by him [the bee] [alone];
she now remembers day and night the essence of love
placed in her heart by that spring. //
If the bee did not desire nectar,
it would not suffer the blow upon the tip of the elephant's ear.
One who approaches others in hope of a particle of pleasure
indeed becomes a receptacle of humiliation. //
O bee, many a flowering vine
with beautifully blossoming tips you have spurned as mere grass!
Now reap the fruit — from these
thorn-covered <s>ketakī</s> (screwpine) vines, O shameless one! //
He who [sported] in the open lotus-hearts of the <s>kamalinī</s>,
who delighted within the buds of the <s>cūta</s> (mango) —
behold now, at the end of autumn, that <s>madhupa</s> (bee) —
his days pass with difficulty in the hollow of a bamboo. //
Having drunk the fragrant nectar of flowers, with pollen as his body-paint,
the bee, seated upon a lotus,
is now trapped by moonbeams and cries pitifully —
whom do misfortunes not visit who lacks contentment? //
On other, more resilient flowering vines, O <s>bhṛṅga</s> (bee),
divert your fickle mind!
Why do you torment, at the wrong time, the young unopened bud,
free of pollen, of the tender <s>navamālikā</s> (jasmine)? //
His body tinged with lotus-pollen clinging
from the shower of <s>mada</s>-drops from <s>Airāvaṇa</s>'s face,
his wings shattered by fierce winds and frost,
the bee, exhausted, lies helpless on the ground. //
Why do you wander about with longing, having lost your composure,
O <s>dvirepha</s> (bee), buzzing pitifully, craving the nectar of flowers?
Fix your resolve upon other trees and vines,
for that blossoming <s>sahakāra</s> (mango) creeper is broken! //
Perfuming all quarters with her fragrance,
red-hued, with a captivating face, of delicate form —
just when the lotus-bud became worthy of attendance,
fate at once carried the <s>madhupa</s> (bee) to another place. //
In a splendid <s>jāti</s> (jasmine), with its sweet, soft, and graceful charm,
two bees entered a lotus at the same time.
One of them, its body full and laden with honey —

children.text: kaṣṭe vidhau na rajasāpi yuto dvitīyaḥ //
children.translated_text: alas, cruel fate! The second did not obtain even the pollen. //
The swarm of bees, leaving the mango, went to the <s>navamālikā</s> (jasmine),
then again went to the <s>raktāśoka</s> and then to the <s>kadamba</s> tree.

children.text: tadapi suciraṃ sthitvā tebhyaḥ prayāti saroruhaṃ
children.translated_text: Having stayed there too for a long while, departing from those, it goes to the lotus —
the world, hating familiar virtues, ever desires what is new. //
On a painted lotus, with one whose soul was utterly captivated by its beauty,

children.text: kimiva na kṛtaṃ tatra bhrāntvā madhuspṛhayālinā /
children.translated_text: what did the bee not do there, wandering about in its craving for honey?
He obtained not a drop of nectar from it — nor was he of small wit —
but at the head [of such fools] the painted one is inscribed by the discerning as [exemplifying] those blinded by desire. //

children.text: bhramati bakule mandaṃ kunde na vindati nirvṛtiṃ
children.translated_text: He roams slowly on the <s>bakula</s>, finds no satisfaction in the <s>kunda</s> (jasmine),
in the naturally fragrant <s>raktāśoka</s> he attains no freedom from sorrow;
with his mind drawn away by longing for the fragrance of sweet flowers in the forest,
the <s>bhṛṅga</s> (bee) grows thin in body, remembering the <s>navamālikā</s> (jasmine). //
Touching gently, kissing, pressing with his limbs,
falling at her feet, he even endeavors to break open her seal;
unable, from the eagerness of heart, to wait for the proper time —
the young bee, having obtained by merit a fresh <s>navamālikā</s> (jasmine) [bud]. //
Seeing the <s>kamalinī</s> (lotus-pond) destroyed by frost, its lotus-stalks ruined,
the <s>dvirephas</s> (bees) at once became lovers of the elephant's temples.
Alas, shame! This is the untrustworthy nature of beings —
no one regards even the memory of former virtues when [the source] is diminished. //

children.text: kimāmodabhrāntyā bhramasi suciraṃ bhṛṅga nanu he
children.translated_text: Why do you wander so long in the delusion of fragrance, O <s>bhṛṅga</s> (bee)?
Do you not know the truth? The summer season burns exceedingly!

children.text: sthitaṃ śūnyaṃ puṣpaiḥ prakaṭaviṭapaṃ paśya vipinaṃ
children.translated_text: See the forest, its branches exposed, empty of flowers —
gone is the glory of <s>Caitra</s> (spring), resplendent and naturally beautiful! //
Who has smelled the noble flower of this one? Who has kissed its stamens?

children.text: pītaḥ kena rasosya kena rajasā codvellitaṃ kena vā /
children.translated_text: Who has drunk its nectar? By whom has its pollen been stirred?
Ho ho, foolish bee, go quickly to other flowering trees!
Here on the <s>pippala</s> (fig) tree, nothing whatsoever can be obtained — it is utterly [barren]! //
Eager, thinking 'Here fresh sweet nectar may be drunk at leisure,'
with heart deceived by the frenzy of thirst, without discerning the truth,
even though weary with fruitless effort, he does not cease — in a painted lotus-pond!
The bee of dull intellect, addicted [to desire], still wanders about, driven by the reservoir of craving. //

children.text: yasyāḥ saṃgamavāñchayā na gaṇitā vāpyo vinidrotpalā
children.translated_text: For whose union he did not regard the pools full of blooming water-lilies,

children.text: yāmāliṅgya samutsukena manasā yātaḥ parāṃ nirvṛtim /
children.translated_text: whom embracing with eager mind he attained supreme bliss —
seeing that sandalwood creeper now broken, that the bee [still] lives —

children.text: dhairyaṃ nāma tadastu tasya na punaḥ snehānurūpaṃ kṛtam //
children.translated_text: let that be called fortitude indeed, but it was not an act befitting love. //

children.text: yenāmodini kesarasya mukule pītaṃ madhu svecchayā
children.translated_text: He who by his own will drank honey from the buds of the <s>kesara</s> (filament),

children.text: nītā yena niśā śaśāṅkadhavalā padmodare śārade /
children.translated_text: who passed moonlit nights in the heart of an autumn lotus,
who roamed on the temple-grounds of elephants wet with <s>mada</s> (ichor) streams —

children.text: soyaṃ bhṛṅgayuvā karīraviṭape badhnātu tuṣṭiṃ kutaḥ //
children.translated_text: how can that young bee now find contentment on a thorny <s>karīra</s> (caper) twig? //
Let there not be death together with this [lotus] — if somehow by fate

children.text: tṛṣṇā vā hatajīvite yadi tadā kiṃ puṣpaśūnyaṃ jagat /
children.translated_text: there is still thirst though life is ended, then is the world devoid of flowers?

children.text: yenaivonmathitaḥ sa eva dayitaḥ padmākaro nirdayaṃ
children.translated_text: That very <s>padmākara</s> (lotus-pond) by which he was tormented is his beloved — mercilessly
the bee, craving the <s>dāna</s>-waters (ichor), follows, alas, that very elephant, being fickle. //
That former reversal of the taste on the tongue, that restlessness of the ears,
that gaze with self and other quarters forgotten in intoxication — what more need be said?
You have ascertained everything about the elephant, O bee — yet [you say]

children.text: vantaḥśūnyakaro niṣevyata iti bhrātaḥ ka eṣa grahaḥ //
children.translated_text: 'He is empty-handed inside, [yet] should be attended' — brother, what is this obsession? //
Ho, ho, <s>bhṛṅga</s> (bee)! Your body wearied by the toil of being buffeted
by the wind from the flapping ears of the <s>mada</s>-blind elephant — why do you sit in vain suffering?
There are at every step fragrant lotus-ponds, their treasuries unlocked
by humming swarms of intoxicated bees, with their contents displayed openly! //
The bee, leaving the fragrance-rich <s>navamālikā</s> (jasmine), went to the <s>yūthikā</s> (jasmine),

children.text: tāṃ tyaktvāpi gataḥ sa candanataruṃ tasmātsarojaṃ gataḥ /
children.translated_text: leaving that too, went to the sandalwood tree, and from there to the lotus.
Trapped there by the moon for long, that dull-witted one cries —

children.text: saṃtoṣeṇa vinā parābhavaśataṃ prāpnoti lubdho janaḥ //
children.translated_text: without contentment, the greedy person meets with a hundred humiliations. //
The night will pass, a beautiful dawn will come,
the sun will rise, and the <s>padminī</s> (lotus) will smile again —
while the <s>dvirepha</s> (bee) thinks thus, enclosed within the bud,

children.text: hā hanta hanta nalinīṃ gaja unmamātha //
children.translated_text: alas, alas, alas! — an elephant uprooted the lotus-pond. //
Wandering in the forest among the forest-blossoms,
the <s>ṣaṭpada</s> (bee) did not smell the <s>gandhaphalī</s> (fragrant fruit-plant).

children.text: sā kiṃ na ramyā sa ca kiṃ na rantā
children.translated_text: Is she not lovely? Is he not a lover?
Overpowering indeed is the will of the Lord alone. //
A fish, reared in the lap [of the lotus], embraced with all its body in infancy,
by <s>Śrī</s>'s (Lakṣmī's) overflowing embrace, with its sheath opening outward,
being drunk unceasingly by motionless bees with fulfilled hopes —
the lotus is gazed upon from afar with unblinking eyes. //
While alive, the crane, swallowing fish, appears like a sage;
but the vulture [hunts only] the dead — shame on false sagehood! //
Standing on one leg as if on a [lotus] stalk, with neck curved,
the old crane creates in young fish the illusion of being a water-lily. //
This crane has suddenly perished —
alas, where now has its [supposed piety] gone?
Well done, O Death!
No one from anywhere is able to deceive you! //
Your own conduct befitting your lineage —
abandoning that, you wish to attain the state of a swan? /
O crane, practice your vow nonetheless,
for it bears fruit — this is [the truth] for men who persevere //
He has not the sweet cooing of <s>kokilas</s> (cuckoos),
nor are his movements graceful like those of swans /
Nor has he the variegated plumage of peacocks —
yet the crane has a virtue: the <s>bakavrata</s> (crane's vow of patient stillness) //
That cleverness of yours in discerning the essence of water mixed with milk,
and also that charming gait delightful with its soft footfalls /

children.text: āstāṃ tāvadbaka yadi tathā vetsi kiṃcidicchlathāśaṃ
children.translated_text: Let those stand for now, O crane — if you know even a little of the art of remaining

children.text: tūṣṇīmevāsitumayi sakhe tvaṃ kathaṃ me na haṃsaḥ //
children.translated_text: silently still, O friend, how would you not be a swan to me? //
'Who are you, with red eyes, beak, and feet?' 'A swan.' 'From where?' 'From <s>Mānasa</s> lake.'
'What is there?' 'Golden lotus-groves, water like nectar,
pearl-oysters, heaps of conches, emerald-growths here and there —'

children.text: chambūkāḥ kimu santi neti ca bakairākarṇya hīhīkṛtam //
children.translated_text: 'Are there any snails?' 'No!' — and hearing this, the cranes burst into laughter //
Equal in color of plumage, black, associated with <s>kokilas</s> (cuckoos) —

children.text: kena vijñāyate kākaḥ svayaṃ yadi na bhāṣate //
children.translated_text: by whom can the crow be identified if it does not speak of its own accord? //

children.text: ātmarutādapi virutaṃ kurvāṇāḥ spardhayā saha mayūraiḥ /
children.translated_text: Competing with peacocks, making sounds louder even than their own [natural] cries —
the wretched crows! How would they know how to produce the <s>kekā</s> (peacock's call)? //
Let him bear a black body, let him peck at excellent fruits,
let him roam in lovely mango-groves /
Let the crow perform the deeds of the male <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo) —

children.text: kākaḥ kila dhvanividhau nanu kāka eva //
children.translated_text: yet in the matter of voice, a crow is indeed a crow //
Having gained proximity by force with the <s>kokila</s> families, beautiful in complexion
and lovely in their tones /
Why did the wretched crow, bereft of charm, with his worth destroyed,
not even manage an imitation of theirs? //
This hamlet is overrun on all sides by <s>Bhillas</s> (tribal hunters),
who relish improper enterprises and are devoted to arrows tipped with poison /

children.text: tarorasya skandhe gamaya samayaṃ kīra nibhṛtaṃ
children.translated_text: O parrot, pass the time hidden upon the branch of this tree —
auspicious speech [is dangerous here]; the seal of silence upon the mouth is the refuge //
He eats excrement taken up in his mouth, leftovers of others' meals,
he scratches the heads of deities with his claws /
He walks shamelessly, [even] suspecting himself a respectable soul —

children.text: kimiva na kurute khaṃ prāpya kāko varākaḥ //
children.translated_text: what indeed does the wretched crow not do upon obtaining the sky? //
Misfortune of speech, impurity of body, rashness in conduct,
suspicion — its very invention is known [to be his], and his livelihood is unspeakable /
Thus, though the crow has abundant [black color] like the fruit of a tree whose branches he has [often] seen,
the wretched one, afflicted, repeatedly swoons at the luster of the <s>kokila</s>'s hue //

children.text: nṛtyantaḥ śikhino manoharamamī śravyaṃ paṭhantaḥ śukā
children.translated_text: Peacocks dancing charmingly, parrots reciting melodiously —

children.text: vīkṣyante na ta eva khalviha ruṣā vāryanta evāthavā /
children.translated_text: are they not seen here? Or rather, are they driven away in anger? /
By this crow, who obtained his lineage through telling tales of coveted gains at the houses of travelers' wives,
this place is now being unrestrainedly enjoyed by the cunning receiver of <s>bali</s> (offerings) //

children.text: re re dhvāṅkṣa virūkṣatāstu vacasaḥ kāṇākṣitā kṣamyate
children.translated_text: 'Ho ho, crow! Let there be harshness of speech; the one-eyed look is forgiven;

children.text: laulyaṃ nāma taveti kātra gaṇanā bhāṇḍyaṃ vibhūṣaiva te /
children.translated_text: your greed — what reckoning is there of that? Buffoonery is indeed your ornament! /

children.text: sarvaṃ soḍhamidaṃ svabhāvavihitaṃ vahnerivauṣṇyaṃ hi te
children.translated_text: All this is endured, being natural to you, like heat to fire;

children.text: yattvevaṃ viguṇasya kāpi bhavato grīvā na tatsahyate //
children.translated_text: but that you, O worthless one, have some kind of neck — that is not tolerable!' //
The crow, having driven away the <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo), savors the fruit of the mango tree;

children.text: bhuṅkte rājaśukaṃ nivārya kuraraḥ krīḍāparo dāḍimam /
children.translated_text: the osprey, having driven away the royal parrot, playfully eats the pomegranate /

children.text: dhūko barhiṇamasya śākhiśikhare śete sajāniḥ sukhaṃ
children.translated_text: The owl, [having driven away] the peacock, sleeps comfortably with its mate on the tree-branch —

children.text: hā jātaṃ viparītamadya vipine śyene parokṣaṃ gate //
children.translated_text: alas, everything has become reversed today in the forest, now that the hawk has gone out of sight! //
Is he adorned with a crest-train like a peacock? Is he a reciter like a parrot?
Is he sweet-voiced like a male <s>kokila</s>? Is he noble-gaited like a swan? /
Is he a source of playful diversion like an ordinary fledgling?

children.text: kākaḥ kena guṇena kāñcanamaye vyāpāritaḥ pañjare //
children.translated_text: By what merit has the crow been installed in a golden cage? //
His birth on the day of the <s>Maruts</s>' (wind-gods') lord, at the renowned festival of the world-age,
his greater fame in the hearing of auspicious chants, his full age and vigor /
His rivalry with <s>Kākutstha</s> (<s>Rāma</s>), such was his astrological knowledge —
it is by that merit that the crow has been placed in a golden cage //
The first moment of the advent of the <s>Kali</s> age has arrived,
when the flocks of swans frequenting great waters are put to shame /
When, at the end of [the last] day of austerities, the one-eyed twice-born (crow)

children.text: kāṇo dvijaḥ pratigṛhaṃ bata yatra pūjyaḥ //
children.translated_text: is summoned with respect and worshipped at every house — alas! //
Whatever is elsewhere in the sun, and whatever in the moon has contact with purpose —

children.text: khadyota iti kīṭasya nāma tuṣṭena kenacit //
children.translated_text: some pleased person gave the name '<s>khadyota</s>' (firefly) to this insect //
That you shine forth in the night when all ten directions are dark with dense darkness — that is one thing;
but now in the daytime, O jewel among insects, your beautiful cool rays are eclipsed by the rays of the stars //
Singeing the tip of a withered blade of grass, not illuminating even a mustard seed —
the <s>khadyota</s> (firefly), self-governing, shines proclaiming its insect-hood //
Radiant in the sky, with much darkness dispelled,
yet of feeble light, with splendor confined to their own body alone /
The fireflies appear of manifest, intense, and weighty power
only so long as the seven-horsed one (the Sun) has not yet risen //
Wretches like you, even worms, were shining
in that night of utter darkness at the close of the age /
Now that the day of sun-rays illuminating the ten directions [has come],
here even the moon does not shine — O jewel among insects, what then of you? //
'The moon will depart, the splendor of the stars will perish,
the gem-lamps licking away darkness will not endure /
The whole [world] will be blind, and then, O jewel among insects,
you will come to open your eyes' — far-fetched indeed is this! //
Whether it be a spark flashing within a creature, or a trifling superimposition of borrowed merit —

children.text: tasmai kātaramohanāya mahaso leśāya mā svasti bhūt /
children.translated_text: may there be no well-being for that particle of splendor which deludes the timid! /
For by this insect named '<s>khadyota</s>' (firefly), glowing red with the flash of its shadow,
we are mocked through the mistaken notion that it is a moving jewel //
The tree is adorned with fresh heaps of leaves alone;

children.text: jahāti jīrṇāṃstāneva kiṃ vā citraṃ kujanmanaḥ //
children.translated_text: it casts off its old ones — what is surprising about those of lowly birth? //
As rich in tender shoots and flowers, as abundant in flowers and fruits,
as fruiting trees become climbers — alas, O mother, where have those trees gone? //

children.text: sādhveva tadvidhāvasya vedhāḥ kliṣṭo na yanmudhā /
children.translated_text: Indeed <s>Vedhas</s> (the Creator) did well for one such as him and was not troubled in vain:
what use would an inappropriate fruit be for the sandalwood tree, whose very form [is its virtue]? //
By me, greedy for jujubes, ignorant of trees,
the <s>khadira</s> (acacia) tree was resorted to in the forest, due to its resemblance to a thorny [fruit-bearing tree] //
Either it becomes a great tree, or it perishes completely, roots and all —
the seedling-sprout of the <s>nyagrodha</s> (banyan) does not undergo the process of [mere] shoots //
With their flowers, leaves, fruits, shade, roots, bark, and timber —

children.text: dhanyā mahīruhā yeṣāṃ vimukhā yānti nārthinaḥ //
children.translated_text: blessed are those great trees from whom no supplicant departs disappointed //
Whether a shower of embers falls or the wind of dissolution blows,
the <s>tāla</s> (palmyra palm), having begun [its growth] in rigidity, perishes with that very [rigidity] //
Giving shade, free of serpents, easy to climb, bearing fruit —
the great roadside trees exist solely for the benefit of others //
No suffering arises from the humiliation of those without recourse;
the <s>aśoka</s> trees, when kicked at the foot, generally become [all the more] full of shoots //
Even though the sandalwood tree has been made devoid of fruit and flower by <s>Vidhi</s> (fate),
it still removes the torment of others by its very body alone //
When the spring month arrives, all the rows of forest trees attain growth;

children.text: yanna karīre pattraṃ tatkiṃ doṣo vasantasya //
children.translated_text: that the <s>karīra</s> (caper bush) has no leaves — is that the fault of spring? //
When the wish-fulfilling tree stands radiant, its dense branches obscuring the bright sunlight —

children.text: chāyārthī kaḥ paśurapi bhavati jaradvīrudhāṃ praṇayī //
children.translated_text: what creature seeking shade would be devoted to withered shrubs? //
When a roadside tree stands nearby, with the stream of sunrays blocked
by hundreds of branches brilliant with fruit, flowers, and tender shoots —
what traveler experiences fatigue? //
Those who, setting aside their own profit, have risen for the quelling of others' torment in this world —
they are trees without refuge [for themselves]; we do not know
even a trace of <s>Prajāpati</s>'s (the Creator's) intention herein //
In the sandalwood, we endure serpents;
whence can a beautiful thing be found without danger? /
Tell me, O <s>khadira</s> (acacia), are these thorns accumulated by you
to protect your own excellence? //
Interlinked with one another, chained
by serpents, climbed upon by the greatly dull —
the sandalwood tree, unresorted to by beautiful flowers,
is therefore not endowed with fruit //
Whatever is even slightly unbecoming, if it accompanies what is fitting —

children.text: kiṃ candanasya na kṛtaṃ kusumaṃ phalaṃ vā /
children.translated_text: has not the sandalwood been given [the absence of] flower or fruit? /
We feel deep shame — let the one who would approach
its vicinity bearing a great axe simply depart //
O young <s>campaka</s> tree, with beautiful flowers worthy of
the pleasure of kissing the grace of a young woman's cheek /
What use is blooming? Abandon the smile of your blossoming here —
this is the region of the desert, [home to] hordes of uncouth commoners //
For the <s>campaka</s> tree whose roots are scorched and burning
within by the heated desert sands — where is the thought of blossoming? /
For those who dwell in a place unsuited to them,
the preservation of one's own life alone is generally the highest good //
The extreme wickedness of <s>Dhātā</s> (the Creator) is proclaimed by himself
in his bestowing fruitlessness upon the birch tree /
Do not its barks, cut into by hundreds of sharp blades,
fulfill the hopes of successive generations of supplicants? //
For what purpose was this <s>khadira</s> (acacia) tree created by the wicked student [of creation] —
one whose sole delight is thorns, who is hostile to fruit,
who stands firmly on the frontier of disagreeableness /
averse to the play of shade, [useless] to the good? //
'Would that which is obtained after long [waiting], like nectar, be for immortality?
Or would it grant a long life like an elixir?'
This is the fruit — that this <s>tāla</s> (palmyra), scorched by the curse of a traveler,
rigid, bears fruit [only] once in a hundred years //
O tree, adorned with the splendor of a heavy burden of great fruits,
renowned throughout the world as the sole queller of the torment of hunger /
From you, by me, somehow only this one small fruit
was obtained below — pecked at by birds and meager //
O tree of agreeable nature, exceedingly cool,

children.text: satyaṃ na kaścidapi te tarurasti tulyaḥ /
children.translated_text: truly no other tree is equal to you /
Yet for those seeking shade too, because of the association of dreadful forked-tongued [serpents],
O sandalwood, you are no different from a poison tree //
How is it that in this vast forest-end, there is not a single noble forest tree
standing tall, rich in flowers, creepers, and fruits? /
By the decree of <s>Dhātā</s> (the Creator), the scorched maker of the world's misery,
only <s>dhava</s>, <s>khadira</s> (acacia), and <s>palāśa</s> (flame-of-the-forest) trees attain growth //
Having found the shade of a tree whose canopy of branches blocked the entire expanse of the sky,
under which the distress of heat was quelled many times by future [travelers] /

children.text: bhoḥ pānthā nanu dṛśyatāṃ vidhigatistasyaiva kālakṣaya-
children.translated_text: O travelers, behold the course of fate — that very tree, now diminished by the decay of time,
its trunk today is merely scorched by the hot sand-embers //
Upon whose branches, with variegated birds having roamed the ten directions, reuniting happily,

children.text: viśrāntaṃ śayitaṃ prabhuktamuṣitaṃ skandhe phalaiḥ praśrite /
children.translated_text: they rested, slept, ate, and dwelt among its spreading fruits /
That very roadside tree, now uprooted by a wicked elephant —
the cowherd boys strip its bark, dry and rough, for fuel //
Is it contentment, or is it inability, or is there no expectation from him?
Is this dwelling in the forest [mere] beauty, or is it aversion? /
Let it be that no connection was made by you, O ill-fated one, with a suitable, fruitful floral splendor —

children.text: saṃbandhonanurūpayāpi na kṛtaḥ kiṃ candanasya tvayā //
children.translated_text: but, O sandalwood, was no connection made even with an unsuitable one? //
Well-rooted, broad-spread, with dense, languid shade, standing on the right path,
'worthy of being served by the good' — thinking thus, the man ascended the palmyra /

children.text: puṃsaḥ śaktiriyatyasau sa tu phaledadyāthavā śvothavā
children.translated_text: A man's capacity is this much [only]; whether that [tree] would fruit today, or tomorrow, or

children.text: kāle kvāpyathavā kadācidathavā netyatra vedhāḥ prabhuḥ //
children.translated_text: sometime, somewhere, or perhaps never — in this, <s>Vidhi</s> (fate) alone is master //
'You were born at a crossroads, you have dense languid shade — what use is shade [alone]?

children.text: saṃyuktaḥ phalitosi kiṃ yadi phalaiḥ pūrṇosi kiṃ saṃnataḥ /
children.translated_text: You have borne fruit — what use if you are full? You are bent [with fruit] —' /

children.text: he sadvṛkṣa sahasva saṃprati sakhe śākhāśikhākarṣaṇa-
children.translated_text: O good tree, endure now, O friend, the pulling of your branches and crown,
the shaking, plucking, and breaking — by the people with their unbridled mischief! //
Of you, whose fine trunk spreads its quality of fragrance, pervading all the quarters with longing,
whose touch has been made between the lovely breasts of a slender woman, whose form is to be protected /
Some fault born of association with serpents has now erupted,

children.text: yena tvāṃ parihṛtya candanataro yāntyadhvagā dūrataḥ //
children.translated_text: by which, O sandalwood tree, travelers pass you by from afar! //
The sandalwood tree, your friend, has been cut down and burned; you serpents came fleeing [here],
accustomed daily to the comfort of coiling — those [former trees] you have forgotten.
If you did not retaliate against that assailant with the flame of poison from your fang-tips,

children.text: kiṃ tenaiva saha svayaṃ na nidhanaṃ yātāḥstha bho bhoginaḥ //
children.translated_text: why did you not perish together with him? O serpents! //
A human lifespan has been spent at your root; let that be considered [well spent] by time.

children.text: ksodīyāṃsamapi kṣaṇaṃ paramataḥ śaktiḥ kutaḥ prāṇitum /
children.translated_text: But henceforth, the power to live even a moment more — whence could it come?
So fare well, grow to great stature — even now, what is our hurry?
O palmyra tree, bear fruit with blessings — in [your] sons or grandsons! //
This shade alone is dense, this fragrance alone dispels the heat of the afflicted,
this alone has the quality of being foremost in virtues — why speak of the sandalwood's excellence?
But from root [to crown], it is so corrupted by serpents that have established their dwelling,

children.text: jāne yena varaṃ dhavotha khadiropyanyothavā na tvayam //
children.translated_text: that I know: better a <s>dhava</s> or even a <s>khadira</s> or any other tree — but not this one! //

children.text: na ślāṣyāni phalāni pallavakṛtā chāyā na vāñchāpi sā
children.translated_text: No delectable fruits, no shade made of tender leaves — nor is that desirable.

children.text: no puṣpaṃ sumanoharaṃ na vihagāḥ śabdāmṛtasyandinaḥ /
children.translated_text: No captivating flower, no birds pouring forth nectar of song.
Beneath this tree of unclean nature, rigid, its aged form laden with crow-droppings —
how, alas, were you created by the wicked Creator? //

children.text: nāsya svāduphalaṃ na cāru kusumaṃ na snigdhaparṇā latā
children.translated_text: No sweet fruit of this one, no lovely blossom, no creeper with glossy leaves,

children.text: na cchāyā klamahāriṇī na ca kalakvāṇāstathā patriṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: no shade that relieves weariness, no melodious birds either.
This is that <s>khadira</s> (acacia) tree — or rather, O traveler, have you seen it?
Then why, O traveler — do you seek wounds on your body from its sharp thorn-tips? //
Lush, full of tender leaves, with broad branches dispelling the fierce sun,
bending low, bearing sweet fruit, relieving the hunger and heat of those who take shelter —
those trees have been burnt! Let the travelers go on those very paths —

children.text: rūkṣāḥ kāṇṭakinaḥ sasarpavivarā bhūyaḥ prarūḍhā drumāḥ //
children.translated_text: harsh, thorny, with snake-holes — [these] trees have grown up again! //

children.text: chāyā nātmana eva yā kathamasāvanyasya niṣpragrahā
children.translated_text: The shade that is not even its own — how can it be freely given to another?
In the calamity of summer heat, on that cool ground, whence would a breeze come?

children.text: vārtā varṣaśate gate kila phalaṃ bhāvīti vārtaiva sā
children.translated_text: The rumor is that in a hundred years it shall bear fruit — indeed, that is just a rumor.

children.text: drāghimṇā muṣitāḥ kiyacciramaho tālena bālā vayam //
children.translated_text: Cheated by its slowness for how long — alas, we have been children deceived by the palmyra! //

children.text: kastvaṃ bhoḥ kathayāmi daivahatakaṃ māṃ viddhi śāhoṭakaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Who are you, sir?' 'Know me to be the wretched <s>śāhoṭaka</s> tree, struck by fate.'

children.text: vairāgyādiva vakṣi sādhu viditaṃ kasmādidaṃ kathyate /
children.translated_text: 'You speak as if with detachment — well said! But why do you say this?'
'Over there on the left is a banyan tree — the traveling folk serve it with their whole being,
yet not even its shade serves the purpose of helping others, though it stands by the road!' //
With fragrance [you give] to the winds, with tender shoots to the deer, with hanging bark to the ascetics,
with flowers to the bees, with fruits to the birds, with shade to those scorched by heat,
with branches to the weary wild elephants — you have always distributed [your gifts].

children.text: prāptastvaṃ druma bodhisattvapadavīṃ satyaṃ kujātāḥ pare //
children.translated_text: O tree, you have truly attained the path of a <s>Bodhisattva</s> — others are of ignoble birth! //
Beneath the shade of those trees whose bases are fragrant with dripping honey from flowers bowed down by swarms of buzzing bees,
throngs of travelers rest as if in their own homes,
ever quenching their thirst with waterfall water and sating themselves with their fruits —

children.text: te nandantu phalantu yāntu ca parāmatyunnatiṃ pādapāḥ //
children.translated_text: may those trees flourish, bear fruit, and attain the highest eminence! //

children.text: he he maṇḍitamārga mārgaviṭapiñjīvyāḥ samāḥ śāśvatīr-
children.translated_text: Ho, ho! O road-adorning tree beside the path, may you live for eternal ages!
Even now, cover the horizons with your branches — your <s>sāla</s> trees have kissed the sky!

children.text: mūle viśramaṇāśayaiva luṭhitā yanna tvayā kevalaṃ
children.translated_text: At your root, as if lying down in a resting place, we were not merely
freed from the heat — we were satisfied with hundreds of your fruits! //
That tree whose growth was prayed for by hundreds of hopeful wishful thinkers —
it has grown, yielding fruit to travelers, a refuge for all who seek shelter.
But an old bird, who came from various lands, by unknown [newcomer] birds now usurped,
though having found his moment, watches from afar. //
Though having endured the pain of forest-fire burning, the affliction of harsh wind and rain, the heat of the sun,
and even the heavy calamity of being uprooted by elephants, and [struck by] the thunderbolt,
they do not withhold from supplicants their wood, shade, fruits, bark, blossoms, flower-clusters, or tender shoots —

children.text: nārthibhyo vārayanti pratidivasamaho sādhu vṛttaṃ tarūṇām //
children.translated_text: day after day — ah, how noble is the conduct of trees! //
Swans desire lotus groves, scavengers and vultures desire flesh,
travelers desire sweet fruits, honey-bees desire sweet fragrance.
From afar, with your heaps of fruitless red flowers, O substance-less, road-elevated,

children.text: re re śalmalipādapa pratidinaṃ ke na tvayā vañcitāḥ //
children.translated_text: ho ho, <s>śalmali</s> (silk-cotton) tree — whom have you not deceived, day after day? //
Brother traveler, thinking this sandalwood tree will end the exhaustion of the fearsome desert wandering,

children.text: matvā candanapādapaṃ pathika mā viśrāntaye śiśriyaḥ /
children.translated_text: do not resort to it for rest!
By the venomous serpents dwelling nearby, terrifying with their streaming flames of dense poison,
how many travelers have been reduced to mere memory! //
He who was sung aloud by swarms of she-bees with minds eager for honey-drinking,
who was made a dwelling by flocks of birds arrived from distant lands,
who was resorted to by hundreds of travelers to dispel the heat of summer —
that same shade-tree has now been destroyed by a maddened elephant! //

children.text: bhuktaṃ svāduphalaṃ kṛtaṃ ca śayanaṃ śākhāgrajaiḥ pallavais-
children.translated_text: Sweet fruit was eaten, a bed was made of the topmost branch-leaves,

children.text: tvacchāyāpariśītalaṃ ca salilaṃ pītaṃ vinītaḥ klamaḥ /
children.translated_text: cool water chilled by your shade was drunk, weariness was allayed.

children.text: viśrāntaṃ suciraṃ tatopi manasā prāptā parā nirvṛtis-
children.translated_text: Having rested long, supreme bliss was attained by the mind.

children.text: tvaṃ sanmārgatarurvayaṃ ca pathikā bhūyāspunaḥ saṃgamaḥ //
children.translated_text: You are a tree on the righteous path, and we are travelers — may there be another meeting! //

children.text: astyeva bhūbhṛtāṃ mūrdhni divi vā dyotatembudaḥ /
children.translated_text: Indeed, a cloud shines either on the peaks of mountains or in the sky.
Though battered by winds, does it ever descend to the netherworld? //
The cloud, having established its place in the firmament,
having filled the ocean with torrents of water —
that it is unable to fill even a cow's hoof-print —
how can this falsehood be uttered? //
This here is the sole sustenance of travelers —
see how the great lake is drying up!
Shame on the foolish rain-cloud, whose good course is blocked —
why was the market-stream augmented here instead? //
Without regard for self-interest, for the relief of the people's suffering,
there are rain-clouds that rise perpetually.
Those who comprehend even the ones that do not rain —
they are indeed certain great souls! //
Where has the blind cloud seen
that grass was grazed down by a cow so that it need not be crushed?
Like a kinsman of travelers, the great tree
arrives, poor thing, with mere dewdrops from the fog! //
Some rivers become [mighty], with waves surging wildly,
by taking shelter at the peaks of lofty mountains.
Others — mere water-drops from grass and clods —
cannot diminish the water of the rain-clouds. //
Where you stayed for a long time, being destitute,
O cloud, a debtor through accepting gifts and taking wealth from the ocean —
you roar shamelessly even at the ocean's shore!
